Titan-Llama applies a blockwise attention mask and preserves full-fidelity attention over recent tokens while compressing historical context into recurrent, fixed-size neural memory modules (NMMs). Our formulation allows pre-trained attention layers to be replaced without training a new language model from scratch. On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Titan-Llama raises accuracy over segmented attention windows from 23.87\% to 40.51\% on QuALITY and from 14.50\% to 40.75\% on LongHealth. Inference benchmarks show more than 20\% faster prefill, 37\% faster decode at medium context lengths, and 24\% lower steady-state decode memory usage in the evaluated configurations. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating memory architecture mechanisms that utilize test-time training effectively modulates long-context behavior of pre-trained models, offering a practical route to adapting pre-trained transformers for efficient long-context inference. Our code is released on Github \href{ this https URL }{GitHub}

title: Diagnosing Low-Confidence Patient Profiles via Localized Harmful Covariate Shift Detection
comment: Accepted at SMASH 2026 (Symposium on Machine Learning and Applications in Healthcare). Code available at this https URL
summary: Before deploying clinical prediction models, their reliability must be assessed to ensure safe use. Errors may arise from distribution shifts between training and deployment or from heterogeneous performance where the model systematically underperforms for certain patient subgroups. Yet most post-hoc diagnostic methods evaluate reliability only at the population level, checking whether the deployment data resemble the training data and whether the model performs well on average, without accounting for heterogeneity that may cause some patients to be disproportionately affected. We propose a unified diagnostic pipeline that combines both perspectives. MED3pa first discovers interpretable low-confidence patient profiles, and Detectron is then applied within each profile to test whether its degradation is associated with a detectable harmful covariate shift. Across three clinical prediction tasks and three injected subgroup shifts in MIMIC-IV, we find that shift detectability itself is informative. An injected age shift, undetectable at the population level, was nonetheless localized to specific degraded profiles, whereas sex- and race-related shifts were detected broadly and therefore offered little guidance for identifying the most affected patients.

title: MA-Bench: Measuring Operational Planning in Language Models
summary: How well can a language model turn a large, incomplete and partly contradictory body of documents into a plan when no single correct answer exists? We introduce Mission Analysis (MA)-Bench, built on mission analysis, the first step of military operational planning, in which a staff reads the full situation and states the problem before anyone proposes a solution. Its 10 expert-built scenarios pair synthetic packets of ten to twelve documents with 1,257 expert-written pass/fail requirements, each containing information on their source, question type, and importance level. A reasoning-model judge grades each brief against the requirements without seeing the documents; it grades like a fifth credentialed planner, leaving a four-planner panel's agreement unchanged (Fleiss $\kappa$ 0.42 to 0.41), and a judge from a second provider reproduces the model ranking (Spearman 0.94). Across twenty frontier and open-weights models the best gets 62% of the rubric items right. Models are strongest on facts stated in the documents (58%) and weakest on judgments that must be inferred (33%), and six failures in ten are omissions rather than errors. MA-Bench grades the determinations, not the prose. We release the packets, rubrics, prompts, scorer and every graded brief with item-level verdicts.

title: CAFE: Confining Feature Distillation to Language-Routed Adapters for Compact Multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition
summary: Feature distillation is usually expected to add to logit distillation. We find that this expectation does not hold for two common feature losses in compact multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR), and analyze why through their gradients. The gradient of a projection-based loss is orthogonal to the task gradient, while that of Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), a similarity-based loss, is weakly aligned with it. CKA lowers the word error rate (WER) on non-English languages, but at the expense of data-rich English. Three loss-level remedies (one trained, two probed) all fall short, and the CKA gradient overlaps with the subspace English uses in the shared encoder by 97.5% to 99.5% (about 81% by chance). Guided by this diagnosis, we propose CAFE (Confined-Adapter Feature distillation), which confines the CKA gradient to adapters that English bypasses, addressing the trade-off in the parameters rather than in the loss. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, CAFE lowers the average WER from 8.55% to 8.02%, beats an adapter-only capacity control at 8.51%, and makes English more stable across checkpoints. At 254M parameters, it trails the 0.6B teacher by 2 WER points and is competitive with much larger models across 48 test sets in 24 languages. We use 564k hours of training data and state-of-the-art models to keep the findings relevant to practice.

title: Imagining Goals with Geometric Horizon Models for Policy Generalization
summary: Training from offline data has allowed for substantial progress in domains such as robotics, leading to general-purpose policies that can be easily applied zero-shot or efficiently finetuned for downstream tasks. However, these policies can still have poor generalization, both due to the choice of modeling objective and from learning from a static dataset. In this work, we focus on the challenging task of zero-shot goal generalization, where a policy is evaluated on unseen tasks that require combining its existing knowledge (compositional generalization). An avenue for improving a policy's generalization is by generating new experience with world models; however, such generation has proven difficult for longer horizons. Thus, to alleviate this issue, we propose TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model and allows for directly imagining novel outcomes that can be achieved by composing existing knowledge. We demonstrate that training on these future outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned BC policies significantly improves generalization in stitching-based OGBench tasks.

title: PairIT: Autoregressive Transformers for Low-Data Molecule Optimization
summary: Generating novel molecules with desired properties is a central challenge in drug discovery. Although foundational work focused on de novo generation, practical use cases require a more complex setting: conditioning on an initial seed molecule, optimizing multiple properties, and operating in data-sparse regimes. We introduce PairIT, a flexible training framework for autoregressive transformers over SMILES sequences that enables seeded generation by learning from pairs of structurally similar molecules. By leveraging matched pairs, the model learns to generate local, chemically meaningful edits that improve a property of the seed molecule. Prompt tokens extend this framework by specifying the target property, desired direction, and approximate magnitude of change. Multiple prompt tokens can be concatenated to enable multi-property optimization at inference time. For properties where pair supervision alone is insufficient, reinforcement learning post-training can further improve optimization, providing a tunable trade-off between proximity to the seed and the optimization objective. PairIT naturally supports pretraining on a large dataset and fine-tuning on a smaller dataset, which is critical for performance in data-sparse regimes. Surprisingly, we observe diminishing returns to the scale of the pretraining dataset. We demonstrate empirically on MoleculeNet and Therapeutics Data Commons datasets that, with appropriate paired-data curation, a standard transformer model of modest size (68M parameters) can achieve robust seeded molecular optimization in low-data regimes.

title: Unlocking Structured Pruning for Reasoning Language Models via Attention-Preserving MLP Trimming
summary: Structured pruning reduces LLM inference costs by removing model components to produce smaller dense models. However, existing methods can cause reasoning performance to collapse on long-form reasoning tasks such as AIME. We propose \textit{LayerTrim}, a training-free structured pruning method that identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features while preserving attention and decoder depth. LayerTrim is the first training-free structured pruning method designed to preserve long-form reasoning without gradients or recovery training. Across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, LayerTrim outperforms existing structured pruning methods in most evaluated settings, improving average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP. On \texttt{Qwen3-14B}, LayerTrim achieves 1.24$\times$ faster prefill and 19.7\% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model, while better preserving reasoning ability. It also achieves the shortest average generation length among evaluated pruned models, while retaining the highest average accuracy. These results demonstrate that LayerTrim improves reasoning efficiency through both structural compression and reduced token generation.

title: Genesis Steering: Better Activation Steering Through Training Data
summary: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time, but its effectiveness depends on the choice of reference data. We introduce genesis steering, which derives a genesis vector from contrastive examples in the model's own fine-tuning data. When these data are unavailable, we draw on the membership inference literature to identify likely training examples and construct a proxy dataset. We establish two theoretical results on optimal displacement to the decision boundary and reduced proxy-estimation bias. We evaluate genesis steering and membership-based proxy construction on Tülu-3-8B, whose fine-tuning data are publicly available, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a control. We find that safety data from Tülu-3-8B's training mixture yield stronger steering than external datasets on both models. On Tülu-3-8B, membership scores largely agree in identifying training examples, and vectors built from top-ranked examples achieve competitive performance against random subsets of the same size. In contrast, the results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct hint that a MIA method will only have a positive effect if the mean direction shift with MIA-filtered in-distribution data is much less severe than the direction shift with OoD data.

title: From Copying to Composition: How Language Models Develop In-Context Learning
summary: In-context learning (ICL) allows language models to adapt their behavior from instructions and demonstrations in a prompt, but accuracy alone does not reveal how contextual information controls their predictions. We study the acquisition and trainability of ICL with a controlled diagnostic that separates copying a nearby demonstration from integrating information across the prompt. Across 17 models, about a third prefer the copied answer, a few are undecided, and the rest prefer the rule-consistent answer, which goes with higher accuracy and with control by the requested value rather than the closest conflicting example. Checkpoint analyses show that models begin prioritizing task-relevant prompt tokens over conflicting examples long before their accuracy improves beyond chance level. In matched training experiments, synthetic documents that define endings and then query them shift models toward compositional responses on the controlled diagnostic, whereas fine-tuning on definition exercises built from rewritten real documents improves accuracy when prompts reassign label meanings. The results suggest that ICL is not acquired as a single, uniform capability. Instead, prompt control, answer preference, construction without candidates, and transfer can develop along distinct trajectories.

title: Beyond Aggregate Accuracy: Item-Level Transitions in Prompt Optimization
summary: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) uses feedback from model responses to improve prompts automatically. However, its effectiveness is usually measured through overall scores, which do not reveal which questions become correct, which previously correct answers become wrong, or whether improvements extend to unseen questions. We introduce Reflective Feedback-Driven Prompt Optimization (RFDPO), a tool that tracks recoveries (incorrect to correct), regressions (correct to incorrect), and churn (all changed outcomes). RFDPO uses this feedback to guide subsequent revisions and records prompt changes throughout optimization. We evaluate RFDPO across five benchmarks covering law, knowledge, instruction following, mathematics, and privacy, using GPT-5 as the optimizer and GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4.1 Mini as solvers. Our results show that overall accuracy can hide substantial changes: in five of nine configurations, churn was at least five times the absolute net change, and a single-item net change concealed up to 17 changed outcomes. Average validation gains were 7.9 percentage points, compared with 5.2 points on held-out tests. In a controlled ablation on LegalBench-Hearsay, item-level feedback reduced churn by 40% ($p=0.024$) while maintaining similar net gains. These findings motivate reporting recovery, regression, churn, and performance on unseen data alongside overall accuracy.

title: Revisiting Generative vs. Dense Retrieval: A Static Value Prior Reverses the Gap
summary: Generative retrieval (GR) has emerged as a strong candidate generator for sequential recommendation as language models and semantic-item identifiers have improved. However, GR is not a uniformly stronger replacement of dense retrieval (DR) in online retail candidate generation. We examine their differences on two Amazon Toys datasets under different metrics. GR leads on best relevant item value among users both methods cover, while DR leads on exact-target recall and relevant value across the ranked list. With deep analysis, we find that popularity contributes the most to GR's measured value lead. Adding the same static item value to DR in one reranking step reverses this lead and keeps recall above GR. Finally, on an industrial-scale internal e-commerce dataset with LLM-judged relevance, we show that a 14B SID-LLM still underperforms a $47\times$ smaller dense encoder.

title: How Inner Optimizers Shape Replica Scaling
summary: Training large language models (LLMs) across geographically distributed and poorly interconnected compute pools or data centers has become a topic of significant interest. This has led to increased study of local optimization methods such as DiLoco for LLMs, especially those that use local (or inner) adaptive or preconditioned optimizers, which are critical for high-performance LLM training. However, a central challenge remains: it is well known that increasing the number of model replicas (replica scaling) while fixing the total training budget leads to monotonically decreasing performance. Existing work has empirically demonstrated that the choice of inner optimizer (Muon v.s. AdamW) can significantly improve this trend, but offers only limited explanation of the performance difference. In this work, we consider a range of inner-optimizers and identify two important factors that impact replica scaling: (1) the covariance structure of the pseudo-gradients and (2) the impact of batch size on the pseudogradient's noise scale. Based on these insights, we theoretically and empirically demonstrate that whitening-based pre-conditioning is a powerful inner-optimizer desideratum. Our empirical evaluation extends the results to reveal that whitening-based inner-optimizers achieve strong replica scaling (for 8-96 replicas), with performance relative to DP improving as parameters and data are scaled.

title: Graph Coarsening Enables Escaping Local Optima in Compute-Constrained Nonconvex MAX-CUT
summary: Because its binary optimization landscape contains exponentially many local optima, MAX-CUT is highly sensitive to initialization. We study Particle Polynomial Relaxation (PPR), a moment-based nonconvex continuous reformulation possessing an advantageous optimization landscape. We warm-start PPR with Combinatorial Multigrid (CMG), a spectral graph-coarsening method that produces structure-aware initial solutions in near-linear time without training data. On \texttt{t2g20} ($n=400$), benchmark instance with known exact optimum, the combined CMG+PPR pipeline reaches $97.5\%$ of optimum on average and $98.4\%$ on the best run. An extended variant with discrete local-search refinement reaches the published optimum on all sixty Biq Mac instances evaluated by a recent neural branch-and-bound method. Using a sparse CSR representation, the same approach scales to G-set instances with up to $20{,}000$ vertices reducing memory requirements by up to $3333\times$ while maintaining a consistent improvement over the CMG warm start. Gains are largest on sparse weighted graphs; on dense graphs we complement the pipeline with spectral sparsification.

title: Loss Curvature as a Sampling-Free Proxy for Memorization in Diffusion Models
summary: Understanding the mechanism behind why diffusion models memorize their training data remains an open question in generative modeling. In this paper, we examine this question from two perspectives: (a) the model-level perspective concerning the onset of memorization in a model during training, and (b) the sample-level perspective concerning the proclivity of an individual sample to be memorized by a given model. We show that the so-called input loss curvature, or the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of the diffusion model's training loss, is an effective metric for quantifying both perspectives on memorization. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that input curvatures averaged across training and validation samples can identify when a model is likely to start regurgitating its training data when tracked over training time. However, this metric is not sufficient for measuring an individual sample's likelihood of being memorized. To address this perspective, we introduce a counterfactual definition of memorization in diffusion models, extending the analogous notion from supervised learning proposed by [Feldman, 2019]. We prove that this counterfactual memorization is controlled by the input curvature of the leave-one-out model, thus establishing a direct theoretical link between a sample's local loss landscape and its generation likelihood. We validate our derived bounds through several empirical experiments and show that input-dependent curvature provides a proxy for memorization.

title: Who Should We Listen to More? Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition for Pluralistic Alignment
summary: Pluralistic alignment needs to accommodate diverse preferences under limited human feedback. Using AI simulators to label preference comparisons reduces annotation costs, but variation in simulation accuracy across individuals can leave some people's preferences poorly represented in training. We study how to allocate human feedback across people to construct training data for pluralistic alignment, and how this allocation affects the trained policy. To make this allocation explicit and controllable, we define a social welfare objective over individual supervision utilities that measure label quality. Each query's marginal welfare gain depends on its expected supervision improvement, the recipient's current utility, and application-designated priority. Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition (WAPA) uses auxiliary reference models to estimate query gains and individual utilities, then selects queries by estimated marginal welfare gain while updating recipient utilities. We prove exact optimality of the acquisition algorithm for the estimated welfare objective under a fixed query budget and model predictions. Experiments on six Roleplay collections and four OpinionQA regions demonstrate improved supervision and controllable allocation tradeoffs. Policy training on four Roleplay collections improves preference prediction for both seen and unseen individuals. When prioritizing a designated group and poorly represented individuals, acquiring human labels for 20% of comparisons recovers 75-86% of the average predictive utility gap between policies trained entirely on AI-generated labels and entirely on ground-truth labels.

title: Scaling Cheap Synthetic Pretraining Improves Indoor Radio-Map Prediction
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. This research was in part sponsored by the HESC MESCS RA grant No. 22rl-052 (DISTAL), and by the NATO Science for Peace and Security Programme under grant ID G9270 (OASIS)
summary: Real measurements are too limited to train an accurate indoor pathloss predictor that works across a wide range of buildings. Large-scale synthetic pretraining offers a way forward, but real building layouts are also scarce, and accurate ray-tracing simulators are slow, expensive, and often proprietary. We address both problems by introducing a generator that automatically creates diverse indoor layouts and a fast, open-source approximate ray tracer that computes radio maps for them. Using this pipeline, we generate 128M synthetic samples, pretrain ResNet-101 and Swin-T encoder-decoders, and fine-tune them on high-quality benchmark data. Despite simulator mismatch, our ResNet-101 model reduces error by 15% on average relative to the best known methods across five indoor radio-map prediction tasks and improves transfer on a small real-measurement dataset. Both architectures show predictable data-scaling trends: power laws fitted on 2M-16M samples predict the mean normalized downstream RMSE at 32M-128M with 3.33% mean absolute percentage error for ResNet-101 and 7.10% for Swin-T. These results show that pretraining on large amounts of cheap simulated data can improve indoor radio-map prediction, even when real measurements and high-quality simulations are limited.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Multilingual Abstractive Summarization: A Comprehensive Study of English and Bengali
summary: Abstractive summarization remains challenging across languages, where linguistic quality and factual consistency may diverge, particularly in low-resource settings. We present a standardized zero-shot benchmark of eight closed-source and open-weight LLMs on size-matched English and Bengali XL-Sum test sets. Our evaluation combines lexical and semantic metrics with reference-free factuality verification and multidimensional LLM-as-a-Judge assessment, providing a comprehensive analysis of both surface-level quality and factual reliability in multilingual summarization. Results reveal substantial cross-lingual variation: GPT-5.6 Luna leads several English lexical metrics but does not maintain the same advantage in Bengali, where LLaMA 3.3 70B achieves the highest ROUGE and BLEU scores. Gemini 2.5 Flash obtains the highest observed Bengali factuality score. Furthermore, evaluation methods produce different model rankings, highlighting the limitations of relying on a single metric for multilingual summarization assessment. These findings demonstrate that strong English summarization performance does not necessarily transfer to Bengali and emphasize the need for comprehensive evaluation frameworks for low-resource languages.

title: Token Utility for On-Policy Distillation via Local Trust-Region Optimization
comment: 10 pages, Accepted to Pre-to-Post workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Token-selection methods for on-policy distillation (OPD) prioritize student-visited positions using diverse signals, including uncertainty, teacher-student disagreement, and mismatch direction. We instead derive token importance from the distillation objective itself: how much can each position's loss decrease under an equal local KL budget on the student's predictive distribution? The answer is the utility $s_t=g_t^\top F_t^\dagger g_t$, where $g_t$ is the logit gradient and $F_t$ is the categorical Fisher matrix. For reverse-KL it equals the student-weighted variance of the student-teacher log-probability ratio, and for forward-KL it equals the Pearson $\chi^2$ divergence, so the appropriate utility follows from the choice of objective. On shared training checkpoints, several independently motivated criteria, including student entropy, KL disagreement, and TIP, concentrate their importance on nearly the same positions as the derived utility at a 50\% selection fraction, while diverging at stricter fractions and for direction-specific criteria. We instantiate the utility as Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW), a continuous, mean-normalized token weighting. Across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 student-teacher pairs, FUW improves over matched uniform OPD under both reverse-KL (1.35-4.0 macro points) and forward-KL (1.08-2.71 macro points), and is competitive with existing selective methods using a single closed-form score derived from the training objective.

title: Following the Flow the Law Requires: Training Voice Agents to Transfer to Unseen Regulated Procedures in Debt Collection
summary: Voice agents built on large language models (LLMs) now handle customer calls, but in regulated applications completing the task is not enough: the agent must follow a conversational flow set by law. In debt collection, it must confirm it is speaking to the debtor before mentioning the debt, identify itself and the creditor, state the amount, and avoid prohibited language. Every creditor turns these rules into its own procedure and revises it. We ask whether a small, self-hosted policy can be trained once and then follow regulated procedures it has never seen. One machine-readable specification per deployment, FlowSpec, generates the policy instruction, gates the tools, supplies the supervision and defines the tests; the agent speaks only approved catalogue sentences. We fine-tune a 9-billion-parameter model on 2,506 conversations from 297 randomized procedures and evaluate a Thai outbound-call agent on four unseen deployment procedures (three debt collection, one non-debt), one from a wholly withheld lineage. Documented checks, fixed by the procedure, rise from 67--71 percents to 93--100 percents, while grounded checks, fixed by the conversation, already pass at 97--100 percents before training; scenario pass rate rises from 15/43 to 40/43. An audit of the shared specification finds 11 defects, 3 of which its own metric did not expose.

title: Do Perturbation Predictors Learn Gene Interactions? Diagnosing Extrapolation in Agentic Screening
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop ML4Molecules: Agentic Systems for Molecular Sciences
summary: High-throughput perturbation screens increasingly use machine-learning models to predict the effects of gene combinations that were never measured. A difficult case arises when both genes in a test pair were seen individually during training, but their combination was not. In this setting, standard OOD methods often fail because neither gene appears unfamiliar on its own. We therefore compare each model prediction with a simple additive prediction obtained by summing the two observed single-gene effects. The difference between them, which we call additive disagreement (AD), measures how much extra interaction effect the model introduces for an unseen combination. Across eight prediction methods and three Perturb-seq datasets, specialised neural predictors do not consistently outperform this simple additive baseline. More importantly, predictions with larger deviations from the additive baseline tend to have larger errors. Conventional output-based and embedding-based confidence signals are inconsistent across datasets and models, whereas AD remains informative across all evaluated compositional settings. We further study how this signal can guide decisions in an agentic perturbation-screening workflow. The code is available at this https URL .

title: Do Vision CIL Methods Transfer to Protein? A Diagnostic Benchmark of Frozen Protein Encoders
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Continual Learning for Foundation Models and Agents (CL4FM Agents)
summary: Protein function annotation operates over an expanding label space, making class-incremental learning (CIL) a natural framework for incorporating newly discovered functions without full retraining. Yet existing CIL methods have been developed largely in vision and have not been systematically evaluated over frozen protein representations. We conduct a controlled benchmark of nine representative CIL methods across five sequence-, structure-, and sequence--structure-based protein encoders and two enzyme function datasets at different scales, while keeping the encoders frozen and evaluation settings consistent across representations. We find that no method transfers reliably across encoders, and that these failures persist across alternative phase constructions. Diagnostic analyses reveal that this instability arises from weak gradient-based stability signals, substantial heterogeneity in embedding geometry, and covariance assumptions whose appropriate capacity changes with both dataset scale and encoder. These findings suggest that the representation itself should be treated as a central component of continual-learning design rather than a passive feature extractor. More generally, reliable protein CIL will require encoder-aware methods that adapt their statistical assumptions and capacity to the geometry of the representation on which they operate. Code is available at this https URL .

title: Inverse Reasoning Models for Efficient Post-Training and Verification from Answer-Only Data
comment: Published at the COLM 2026 Workshop on Efficient Reasoning
summary: Post-training reasoning LLMs often requires making a tradeoff between costly supervision and compute inefficiency: supervised finetuning typically requires reasoning traces, which is data inefficient since in many applications one only has prompt-answer tuples and lacks the groundtruth chain-of-thought (CoT) sequence. On the other hand, reinforcement learning (with verifiable rewards, for example) can operate without CoT data but it is much more compute-inefficient since it requires multiple autoregressive completions per optimization step, none of which are guaranteed to give a non-zero policy gradient. In this work we explore a middleground, a self-distillation technique that uses answer-only data, treating CoT as latent variables. This relies on training a partner ``inverse reasoning LLM" that generates the original's reasoning traces conditioned on the answer. The inverse model is trained once and reused across incoming batches of answer-only data, with all generation happening offline and up front, making the approach particularly suited to continual post-training. Using Qwen3-0.6B on the Countdown and GSM8K tasks, we show that after GRPO training has saturated, a single offline distillation round from the inverse model roughly doubles pass@1 on hard prompts and, on Countdown, outperforms rejection-sampling self-distillation on every hard-tail metric at every mix ratio (with smaller gains on GSM8K); rejection sampling by construction has no signal on problems the model never solves on its own. Continued GRPO on the fresh data retains an edge at hard pass@1 but trails distillation at pass@8 and pass@32 while regenerating rollouts at every step. As an added bonus we see that the inverse model has a second application as an accurate verifier of correctness. When used for best-of-$n$ selection at test time, it raises selection accuracy on Countdown from 0.753 (majority voting) to 0.969.

title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
summary: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs. Although such supervision encourages linguistic representations, it does not explicitly require them to preserve information about how the underlying time-series signal evolves. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in LOTUS, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, LOTUS achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that LOTUS uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25 to 50 times their size on TSRBench.

title: Understanding NVIDIA Grace-Blackwell Unified Memory Through Placement-Controlled Microbenchmarks
summary: NVIDIA Grace--Blackwell systems make CPU--GPU memory increasingly unified at the programming level, but unified addressability does not make the memory system uniform. A CUDA managed allocation on GB200 may be served from GPU-local HBM, accessed through host/system memory, demand-migrated, prefetched, reused after GPU access, or evicted and reloaded under capacity pressure. The problem is that these states share a programming interface while exercising different hardware paths and runtime mechanisms, making a single ``Unified Memory bandwidth'' number misleading. This paper presents a placement-controlled microbenchmark study of CUDA Unified Memory on NVIDIA GB200, using GH200 as a Grace--Hopper baseline and GB10/DGX Spark as a validation platform. Our methodology separates local HBM access, host/system-memory access, explicit movement, managed first touch, prefetch, reuse, access-pattern sensitivity, oversubscription, and CPU--GPU handoff, then summarizes the observations with a measurement-calibrated model of compute, access, migration, eviction, synchronization, and handoff costs. On GB200, a 1~GB STREAM-style triad reaches 3963~GB/s from local HBM but 304~GB/s through host-mapped CPU/system memory; for a 256~MB streaming kernel, cold CPU-initialized managed memory reaches 14.1~GB/s, while managed prefetch and reuse reach 4606~GB/s and 4504~GB/s. Below the capacity boundary, prefetched and reused managed memory remain above 4.6~TB/s, but at 125\% of CUDA-visible memory they fall to 968~GB/s and 1214~GB/s, showing that Grace--Blackwell unified memory must be understood through placement, access history, locality, reuse, and capacity pressure.

title: TrimSO(2): Fast and Memory-Efficient Training of Equivariant Interatomic Potentials
summary: Equivariant interatomic potentials enable accurate and efficient simulations of molecules and materials. Among them, models based on SO(2) convolutions reduce the cost of tensor products and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy, but their training remains time-consuming and memory-intensive. Existing training implementations materialize large edge tensors for representation transformations surrounding dense matrix multiplications, increasing memory usage and data movement. We observe that these transformations can be integrated into the model's existing dataflow, avoiding separate intermediate materialization. We introduce TrimSO(2), a fast and memory-efficient algorithm for SO(2)-based equivariant models. It realizes this principle through rotation on gather, recombination with activation, and inverse rotation on reduction, with support for the higher-order differentiation required for training. By avoiding intermediate materialization, TrimSO(2) delivers 2.71-16.73$\times$ operator speedups across forward, backward, and double backward and reduces model-level high-bandwidth memory traffic by 3.81-9.88$\times$. Finally, TrimSO(2) achieves 2.07-2.94$\times$ training speedups and 1.53-3.16$\times$ reductions in peak training memory over PyTorch implementations for official eSEN, UMA, and EquiformerV3 workloads on A100 and H100 GPUs.

title: JointServe: Serving Multi-Model Agents on Memory-Constrained GPUs
summary: LLM agents are evolving from a single model calling tools to planners that orchestrate multiple expert models whose capabilities live in distinct weights. This shift breaks a hidden assumption of today's serving systems: that the working set of models fits in GPU memory. On the memory-constrained GPUs typical of private and edge deployments, naive whole-model swapping serializes weight transfer with computation and, without host-backed KV restoration, discards session state at a switch. We present JointServe, a serving system that treats weight shards and KV blocks as residency objects competing for one unified memory budget. JointServe exploits three structural properties of agent workloads (directed calls, gapped execution, and dual-state residency) to prepare models before they are called: an intent signal parsed from the caller's own output stream triggers prefetch during generation, partial k* residency reduces switching to incremental layers, and a preemptive transfer scheduler protects live-session KV with a guaranteed bandwidth share. A carve-out control step adjusts the weight/KV allocation as workload demands change. Evaluations show that JointServe reduces session completion time by 21.7% over the strongest whole-model swap baseline and stays usable in a crash regime where every whole-model swap baseline fails to finish (a 46-fold gap). On replayed SWE-bench, tau-bench, and OSWorld traces, it cuts session completion time by up to 49% and lifts SLO attainment from 2.8-24.5% to 76.8-100%.

title: The Cost of Context: Profiling the Energy Footprint of Input Tokens in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted at HotCarbon'26, the 5th Workshop on Sustainable Computer Systems; to appear in ACM SIGENERGY Energy Informatics Review, Vol. 6, Issue 2
summary: The rapid adoption of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and long-context LLMs has shifted the computational burden toward the prefill phase---the initial stage where the model processes all input tokens in parallel before generating a response---yet its energy impact remains poorly characterised. We investigate the contradiction between massive hardware-level power spikes and the sub-linear marginal cost of input tokens reported in system-level studies. Through high-resolution telemetry of Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2 models on NVIDIA A100 hardware, we identify the efficiency threshold where $O(n^2)$ attention complexity overcomes GPU parallelisation. Our results quantify how optimised memory orchestration (PagedAttention) delays this scaling bottleneck across three orders of context scaling, yielding up to an 8.9$\times$ energy efficiency advantage at 112,000 tokens compared to standard baselines. Furthermore, we characterise the energy disparity between input and output tokens, demonstrating that optimised serving (vLLM) causes this ratio to narrow (from $\approx$850$\times$ to 750$\times$) as context scales due to high decode efficiency, whereas unoptimised baselines show a much smaller, roughly constant gap ($\approx$150--230$\times$) because their prefill is itself expensive. This work establishes context-scaling laws that differentiate engine-level optimisations from inherent model constraints, providing an empirical framework for sustainable LLM deployment.

title: Parallel Sparse Outputs for Tensor Compilers
summary: Sparse tensor compilers are commonly used high-performance tools that optimize tensor algebra programs over notoriously complex sparse data structures. Despite the ever-increasing size and scale of sparse datasets, there exists astonishingly little research on developing a parallel sparse tensor compiler. Existing approaches fail to parallelize or make assumptions about access patterns or output formats that limit generality. This paper presents Birdseed, the first tensor compiler to support all loop orderings over any standard sparse format in parallel. More specifically, Birdseed supports parallel sparse scatters and directly writes into list, bytemap, hash, and dense levels of fibertree sparse formats. Our approach exhibits asymptotic memory and time improvements over all previous work. We additionally demonstrate empirical speedups on challenging kernels to parallelize, such as histogram construction and SpMSpV.

title: Delta Tokenizer: Reference-Identical Tokenization of Session Deltas and Segment-Parallelism for Long Prompts on Multicore CPUs
comment: 42 pages (16-page main text, references, and supplementary material), 14 figures, 35 tables. The incremental tokenization path and the fast encoder are open source in toktier at this https URL . The chunk-parallel path, the CPU pool scheduler, and the SGLang adapter will be released in the same repository
summary: An agent that drives an LLM sends the model the same conversation again and again, and each turn adds only a little text at the end. Inference engines reuse the KV cache of the shared prefix, so only the new tokens pass through the model. However, tokenization has no such shortcut. The CPU front end of the serving engine converts every request back into token IDs from its first character, which lengthens the time to first token (TTFT) and consumes CPU on every turn. We present Delta Tokenizer, a CPU tokenization front end that tokenizes only the delta between a request and the previous request of the same session. It retains the earlier token sequence, encodes again only the appended text and the short tail whose tokens the append could affect, and joins the two only at a position the tokenizer's splitting rules themselves cannot move, which keeps the result exact. For long requests with no state to reuse, it cuts the text where practical tokenizers already keep neighboring pieces independent, encodes the pieces on several cores at once, and concatenates the outputs into the reference encoding, exactly. A shared CPU pool schedules these chunks together with the short incremental updates, so an update runs between two chunks rather than behind an entire long job. The incremental path shortens the tokenization of a session turn by roughly 40x relative to the Hugging Face reference tokenizer, and on 16 cores the chunk-parallel path encodes a four-million-character request 8.2x faster than a serial encode and 1.6-2.1x faster than LoPT. Inside SGLang, Delta Tokenizer reduces the median TTFT through the chat interface by 59% at 100K tokens and brings the P99 TTFT of agent sessions down 9.5x under load and 23x when long requests tie up the front end. Every output we checked matches the reference, among them 41.8 billion documents encoded by its fast encoder.

title: Dynamic 3-Coloring of Bipartite Graphs with Optimal Locality
summary: We give a dynamic graph algorithm which maintains a 3-coloring in bipartite graphs under edge insertions such that the coloring only changes within a radius of $O(\log n)$ around an inserted edge. In the context of locality theory in distributed graph algorithms, this gives an upper bound on the locality under the dynamic-LOCAL model. Our bound on the locality is tight, as the problem admits a matching $\Omega(\log n)$ lower bound in the stronger online-LOCAL model, by a result of Chang et al. [PODC 2024]. Thus, our result closes the gap between dynamic and online locality of this problem.

title: What Should a Software Team Spend on Agents? Simulation-Based Cost Optimization of Mixed AI-Human Teams
summary: Context: AI agents are rapidly adopted in software development, but their token costs are rising and it is unclear how much a team should spend on agents, and on which tasks. Objective: We determine how teams should divide spending between human developers and AI agents to deliver the features a project demands at the lowest total cost. Method: We model mixed teams of human developers and AI agents with eight specialized roles as a discrete-time stochastic process covering bug injection and detection, technical debt, human supervision of agents, and release cycles with feature freezes. Using Monte Carlo simulation and evolutionary search, we determine cost-optimal teams for 432 scenarios varying developer capability, project velocity, debt dynamics, agent capability and price, and bug costs, and compare them with a human-only baseline. Results: Escaped bugs are the dominant cost driver, and 61% of the agent budget goes to finding bugs. Agent capability matters more than token price, since higher-quality outputs reduce downstream quality assurance costs. In teams with capable agents, human developers mostly fix bugs and leave the implementation of new features to the agents. Teams with high-capability agents are typically cheaper than human-only teams, but low-capability agents offer no consistent advantage. At realistic velocities, the optimal teams still spend more on developers than on agents. Conclusions: There is neither a universal token budget per developer nor a universal agentic team structure. As in traditional development, this depends on many factors and teams need to be carefully tailored to the project context to achieve the optimal cost-quality trade-off.

title: The Code of Theseus: Can Agents Rebuild Software from Recovered Design Documents?
summary: LLM agents increasingly design a system before implementing it, yet the data to train and evaluate them centres on implementation and testing: requirements and design artefacts are often missing, outdated or private. Source code, in contrast, is abundant. Prior work recovers architecture documentation by feeding LLMs the source code or letting agents explore it, which saturates the context, does not scale to many repositories, and yields a single artefact rather than aligned ones. We present a framework that recovers aligned stakeholder intent, requirements and architecture from a compact repository representation, a static dependency graph and key contextual files, and release the artefacts of 10,764 Java, Python, C/C++ and C# repositories as a dataset. An LLM judge rates the artefacts of three generators as clear and internally consistent, but less reliably correct and at the right level of abstraction. To test whether the artefacts carry the design, we pose a software Ship of Theseus: a coding agent rebuilds 29 Commit0 libraries from the intent alone or with the recovered requirements and architecture, given only an interface contract and part of the tests. The artefacts do not significantly change the held-out pass rate (33.7% vs. 35.8%), but bring the rebuilt module structure significantly closer to the original (module F1 from 0.54 to 0.63), with either generator and even with concise artefacts. Recovered artefacts thus convey design that tests do not capture, offering a scalable source of design-level data for agents that design before they implement, and the round trip measures this without human references.

title: LintEval: Benchmarking LLMs on Linter-Guided File Refactoring
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. Code available at this https URL
summary: Linters are widely used in code maintenance and real-time IDE editing to surface lint alerts related to performance, style, error-prone, and other patterns in source files. However, existing code benchmarks do not explicitly evaluate linter-guided file refactoring, where models must reduce lint alerts in source files with correct initial functionality while satisfying functionality preservation. We introduce LintEval, a multilingual benchmark for linter-guided file refactoring across C++, Python, and Java, comprising 13,061 programs with correct initial functionality and 171,662 lint alerts extracted using language-specific linters. LintEval jointly evaluates functionality preservation, lint alert reduction, new alert avoidance, and edit minimality. Experiments reveal a persistent trade-off: closed-source commercial models reach up to 90.4% Reduction@P but achieve only 67.1%-68.3% Pass@1, while several open-source small models show low or negative Reduction@P. A controlled fine-tuning study further shows that supervision format matters: refactoring-oriented SFT raises Qwen2.5-Coder-7B Reduction@P from 24.7% to 76.0%. LintEval enables controlled evaluation of models that improve source files under functionality preservation.

title: Temporal Adaptive Fine-Tuning for Code Comprehension
summary: Repository-level code comprehension question answering (QA) supports developer reasoning over functionality and usage distributed across codebases. However, repository-specialized large language models (LLMs) can become misaligned as code evolves. We study this challenge as temporal repository adaptation: acquiring new knowledge, suppressing obsolete, retaining still-valid, and preserving semantically neighboring knowledge. Existing retrieval, fine-tuning, and model-editing methods address only parts of this problem. We propose Temporal Adaptive Fine-Tuning (TAFT), a novel adaptation approach that treats repository transitions as supervision. TAFT derives temporally grounded QA data from repository transitions, pairs newly valid with obsolete knowledge through preference optimization, and replays transition-conditioned retention examples to preserve still-valid knowledge. We evaluate TAFT on an augmented temporal SWE-bench dataset comprising 255,295 QA entries across ten temporal slices, comparing deferred (Baseline), per-slice retrained (Baseline-Batched), and variants with knowledge anchors along four dimensions: updated knowledge, obsolete-answer suppression, retention, and neighbor stability. TAFT consistently outperforms both the deferred and batched baselines, with an average relative improvement of 18% in updated/suppressed knowledge accuracy, doubled retention accuracy, and roughly 1.5 times the neighbor accuracy. With directly supplied knowledge anchors, TAFT-KANT further improves mean updated/suppressed, retention, and neighbor accuracy over TAFT by 3.55%, 8.35%, and 13.00%, respectively. Overall, TAFT demonstrates its effectiveness across all evaluated areas, effectively enabling code comprehension QA alignment with repository evolution.

title: Taming the Online Software Engineering Tongue: Detecting and Reducing Offensive Language in Software Communities
summary: Online Software Engineering (SE) communities such as Stack Overflow have become unwelcoming and hostile spaces, as evidenced by the presence of rude and offensive comments that are detrimental to the emotional wellbeing of participants. The main objective of this work is to investigate the prevalence and nature of offensive language in online SE communities, and develop approaches to classify them with the ultimate goal of reducing offensive language by proposing an Offensive Language Reduction System (OLRSSE) that has the ability to detect, classify, and explain to the poster why a comment is offensive and also propose non-offensive alternative suggestions. Using data from 130,000 user comments on discussions held in four prominent SE platforms: Stack Overflow, GitHub, Gitter and Slack, we developed six sets of twelve (72 in total) different machine learning models (both traditional and deep learning). The F1-Score of the best performing models in the system ranges from 0.56 to 0.94, with an average F1-Score of 0.85, predominantly using BERT as the primary model for various classification tasks. Also, two language-based models were developed for paraphrasing offensive to non-offensive comments. The overall utility of the OLRS-SE was evaluated using user studies with 30 participants, which showed that the developed system is easy to use and also effective in reducing offensive language. Investigating the capabilities of different large language models for offensive language reduction is a promising avenue for future research.

title: Systematic Detection of Energy Regressions in Software Version Histories
comment: 17 pages, 4 figures, submitted to Information and Software Technology journal
summary: Context: Green software engineering is emerging as a crucial response to the rising energy impact of information technology, especially in continuous development. However, challenges remain in devising automated methods to efficiently identify energy regressions across commits. In particular, little effort has been put into automatically detecting regressions at the commit level by identifying statistically significant changes in energy consumption. Objectives: This paper presents EnergyTrackr, an approach for detecting energy regressions across multiple commits. Methods: We empirically evaluated EnergyTrackr on 1,932 commits from five Java projects, assessing its ability to identify significant energy changes. We also compared a straightforward linear algorithm that analyzes the entire commit history with a more efficient dichotomous search algorithm. Results: The evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of EnergyTrackr in identifying significant energy changes across commits. Our findings highlight the efficiency of the dichotomous algorithm in uncovering overall software energy trends, achieving results comparable to the linear approach while reducing resource consumption and processing time. Conclusion: We expect EnergyTrackr to help developers accurately monitor energy regressions and improvements in their projects and optimize their source code to reduce software energy consumption.

title: When Does the Dependency Graph Help Code-to-Architecture Mapping?
summary: Architectural technical debt arises when a system's implementation drifts from its inten ded modular decomposition, while the mapping between source files and architectural modu les is missing, incomplete, or costly to maintain manually. We formulate code-to-archite cture mapping as semi-supervised node classification over a directed multi-relational de pendency graph, with files as nodes, typed dependencies as edges, and lexical features d erived from code identifiers and directory layout. Starting from a small labeled sample, an iterative self-training procedure expands the mapping to the remaining files. We com pare a graph convolutional network (GCN), a graph attention network (GAT), and a graph-f ree multi-layer perceptron (MLP), using identical features and training procedures for t he learned models, against a Naive Bayes reference. Across 100 runs on ten open-source J ava and C/C++ systems, all three neural models outperform the reference on both F1 metri cs. GAT achieves the highest averages of system-level median macro and micro F1, at 83.5 and 92.2, respectively, whereas MLP remains competitive or superior on several systems. On Chrome, the largest system with 18,343 files, GAT and GCN exceed MLP by 22 and 19 ma cro-F1 points, respectively, and have substantially fewer persistently misclassified fil es. Connectivity and homophily are associated with where neural message passing helps, w hile multi-relational aggregation outperforms a single merged edge type on every system for both GCN and GAT. A follow-up study finds that several model rankings depend on the training seed, qualifying smaller advantages without removing the large graph benefit ob served on Chrome.

title: BenchChecker: Assessing the Credibility of Bug-Fixing Benchmarks for LLMs
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for Automatic Program Repair (APR), existing benchmarks suffer from data contamination, in which test samples appear in training sets, artificially inflating performance. To address this, we propose BenchChecker, a framework compatible with both open-source and closed-source models that supports more credible evaluation by detecting such contamination. Grounded in the observation that persistent patches likely remain in recent repository snapshots used for training, BenchChecker employs a forensics-based two-stage detection process using only textual model outputs together with public repository history. The first stage conducts a repository presence test by probing the model with code prefixes to infer training inclusion; the second stage performs a patch presence test to verify patch persistence via similarity alignment and test-suite verification. Evaluations using StarCoder-15B, StarCoder2-15B, and CodeGen2-16B trained on The Stack v2 demonstrate that BenchChecker achieves robust detection with AUC scores around 0.9 across six benchmarks. Furthermore, applying BenchChecker to SWE-bench Verified and Multi-SWE-bench reveals that filtering contaminated samples reduces the reported resolution rates of most LLMs by more than 20% relative to the original rates on medium-difficulty tasks.

title: OS-Bench: Evaluating SWE Agents on Cross-OS Code Migration
summary: Language-model (LM) agents are increasingly evaluated on repository-level software engineering (SWE) benchmarks derived from GitHub issues and pull requests. Although these benchmarks cover a broad range of development tasks, they provide limited insight into a common yet technically distinct challenge: migrating an existing implementation from one operating system (OS) to another while preserving behavior on both. We introduce OS-Bench, an executable benchmark for cross-OS code migration between Linux and Windows. Motivated by case studies showing that cross-platform features are frequently implemented on one OS before support is added for another, OS-Bench identifies migration opportunities by comparing execution coverage collected from the same repository on both systems. Platform-specific regions are then verified, organized into five migration scenarios, and transformed into repository-level tasks with target-platform tests and source-platform regression tests. The resulting benchmark contains 140 validated tasks from 111 repositories across C, C++, C#, Go, and Rust, comprising 91 Windows-to-Linux and 49 Linux-to-Windows migrations. We evaluate six models with SWE-agent, Claude Code, OpenHands, and Win-agent. The best configurations achieve only 26.4% success on Linux-target tasks and 20.4% on Windows-target tasks while preserving correctness across both systems. These results indicate that cross-OS migration is a challenging and underexplored capability, and OS-Bench is a testbed for improving platform-aware SWE agents.

title: Beyond Functional Correctness: Static Code Quality Profiling of LLM-Generated Code
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for code generation, yet most evaluations still focus on whether generated code passes benchmark test suites. Functional correctness alone, however, provides only a limited view of quality: benchmark tests are often incomplete, and passing them does not guarantee that code is maintainable, reliable, or well-structured. This paper {presents a large-scale static quality profiling of} LLM-generated Python code, with a focus on maintainability and reliability. Using 65{,}663 programs from 73 models in LiveCodeBench, we evaluate generated code with established static analysis tools, including Pylint, Radon, and SonarQube. Our results show systematic differences across models that are not captured by correctness alone, with maintainability emerging as the clearest source of variation. We further find that correctness often comes with structural trade-offs rather than uniformly simpler solutions. Overall, our findings motivate evaluation frameworks that assess LLM-generated code beyond pass rates alone.

title: DivAlgo: A systematic evaluation of algorithmic diversity for code generation models
summary: Code generation models are actively being used in professional and educational settings. However, the competence of large language models (LLMs) to generate algorithmically diverse code remains largely unknown. We propose the DivAlgo benchmark, a large-scale dataset constituting algorithmically diverse solutions to programming problems. We also introduce a lightweight similarity metric to enable large-scale evaluation. Our experiments across 24 modern code generation models found that uncontrolled model-generated code is significantly less diverse than human solutions (capturing ~31% of human diversity), and even the best diverse code generation strategy could achieve only ~70% of human diversity. Moreover, while it was possible to steer the models to generate solutions based on human strategies, they were unable to reproduce the diversity of the human solutions. These findings indicate the limitations of code generation models in capturing the algorithmic diversity humans exhibit, and that overexposure to model-generated code can narrow programmers' algorithmic vocabulary.

title: A Systematic Study of Deprecated Android API Usage Updates
summary: Android Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) continuously evolve, causing existing APIs to become deprecated and requiring developers to migrate their usages to recommended replacements. Although prior studies have proposed automated migration techniques, their effectiveness is often limited by the diversity and contextual complexity of API changes. This paper presents a systematic study of deprecated Android APIs, their recommended replacements, and real-world usage updates performed by developers. Based on an analysis of 1,000 deprecated APIs and 4,336 migration examples collected from GitHub, we identify six migration categories and derive recurring usage-update patterns involving Android-version checks, parameter adaptation, object initialization, data-type conversion, and changes in API interaction mechanisms. To assess their applicability, we augment the zero-shot GUPPY benchmark prompts with the migration category and corresponding usage-update pattern. On 156 benchmark tasks, the pattern-guided prompt improves correct updates from 139 to 147 and performs better in five of the six categories.

title: Learnable Hodge-Laplacian Driven Mixture of Experts for Steady-PDE Surrogates on Coarse Unstructured Meshes
summary: Current approaches for steady partial differential equations surrogate models on unstructured meshes apply a single mixing mechanism to the whole solution. This paper proposes an architecture that partitions the solution among vanilla transformer experts, each focused on a different spectral scale. The partition is built from a discrete Hodge Laplacian $L_0=\star_0^{-1} d_0^{\top}\star_1 d_0$, that serves as a fitting layer measuring high-frequency content. A gating mechanism takes the mesh as input and produces the per-vertex weights that recombine the expert outputs. AirFRANS is a steady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) airfoil benchmark. We evaluate our approach in a reduced remeshed version of the benchmark with each unstructured mesh counting 9.6K faces and 4.9K vertices. We compare our approach with the Transolver on the same dataset and dataset slit. Our approach reduces relative $L_2$ error by 31\% and interior mean squared error by 47\%.

title: Revisiting Simple Baselines for Relational Deep Learning
summary: Relational deep learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning end-to-end predictive models over relational databases by representing them as temporal heterogeneous graphs. Recent advances based on graph neural networks and Transformers have achieved strong performance across diverse domains. However, the effectiveness of simpler relational baselines remains underexplored, making it difficult to assess how much architectural complexity is needed to achieve strong predictive performance. Motivated by the observation that predictive signals arise from target attributes, relational attributes, and historical labels, we revisit how effectively these signals can be exploited using simple propagation methods. We adapt fixed low-pass feature propagation to relational entity graphs and train an MLP for prediction. The resulting predictions are further refined using Correct-and-Smooth, a graph-based label propagation algorithm that incorporates historical labels over task-specific meta-graphs connecting target entities. Across classification and regression tasks on RelBench, an MLP trained on neighborhood-filtered features outperforms one using only target-entity features on most tasks and recovers a substantial portion of the performance of heterogeneous GNNs. Correct-and-Smooth provides further gains from historical labels, although applying it requires a separately constructed meta-graph because connections among target entities are not directly specified by the relational entity graph. Together, our studies revisit the effectiveness of established propagation methods as simple RDL baselines while identifying canonical meta-graph construction as a key challenge for effective label propagation.

title: Generative Representation Learning for Scalable Latent Tokenization
summary: We introduce an approach for self-supervised representation learning designed to be used as a tokenizer for generative modeling. Our objective supervises a representation loss by factorizing the pointwise mutual information of the data, which we estimate by taking information differences between conditional predictions from a learned generative model. We justify our algorithm theoretically and empirically, demonstrating that our generative approach to representation learning avoids dimensional collapse and feature suppression in cases where commonly used methods like DINO and LeJEPA fail. Moreover, we show our representation learning technique is scalable; expending more compute leads to predictably better latent tokenization. For the first time, we perform a careful analysis of the combined flop efficiency of tokenizer and generative model and demonstrate that our approach is a compute-optimal improvement over direct diffusion for pixel-space generation, obtaining an FID-50K of 2.18 with JiT-L. Applied to ImageNet and the text-to-image dataset GPIC, we show tokenizer encoder scaling laws for diffusability, where extrapolating our approach achieves representations in 7x fewer FLOPs than DINOv2 on ImageNet and 8x fewer FLOPs than WebSSL on GPIC.

title: The Physics Is the Network: Fast, Training-Free Neural Emulation
summary: Neural emulation need not require learning a substitute for known physics. We investigate PolyNets that couple a continuous-time neural representation of polynomial dynamics with a simple recurrent network for discrete-time integration. When the governing coefficients are known, the resulting tensor graph requires no training and preserves the prescribed numerical scheme while enabling efficient hardware execution and parallel simulation. Using the one-dimensional Korteweg-de Vries equation, we compare PolyNet with CPU and GPU finite-difference Runge-Kutta solvers and three trained neural models: a state-map emulator, a physics-informed predictor, and a learned-tendency integrator. Analytical soliton solutions provide a reference for amplitude and phase errors across grid resolutions, 10^6 dispersively scaled time steps, ensembles of up to 10^4 trajectories, and varying initial amplitudes. PolyNet achieves accuracy comparable to the numerical solvers, including at amplitudes outside the learned models' training conditions. It combines this fidelity with high GPU throughput, approximately constant over the tested resolution range, and favorable ensemble scaling.

title: Bayesian Learning to Select Fair Classifiers
summary: Evaluations of classifiers (AI or human or agents) often assume a batch setting in which every agent produces labels on every example in a test set, which can be expensive or impractical in many contexts. This motivates online policies that adaptively select agents to query as examples arrive and update policies as outcomes are observed. We study the problem of selecting, in an online stream, the agent that best balances (i) predictive performance and (ii) subgroup fairness of a sensitive attribute, and that allows for delayed observations of true class labels. We formulate this as a Bayesian multi-armed bandit problem using Thompson Sampling, explicitly balancing accuracy and fairness. We conduct empirical evaluations on real-world datasets spanning problems involving tabular classifiers, large language models, and human labelers, demonstrating substantial reductions in regret relative to baselines. Our theoretical contributions include guarantees on the performance of the selected agent that incorporate both the accuracy and fairness aspects of the problem.

title: A Two-Level Clinical Novelty Prioritization Framework for Disease Trajectories Discovered from Longitudinal Electronic Health Records
summary: Graph-based analysis of electronic health records (EHRs) yields disease-trajectory catalogs, but structural support does not establish semantic novelty. We present a two-level framework to prioritize 99,527 branching motifs previously discovered by an upstream patient-disjoint, train-only MIMIC-IV v3.1 pipeline and frozen after validation-based catalog selection. The framework separates path-level and node-to-endpoint semantic sparsity from reliability-adjusted clinical priority. Three deterministic textualizations per motif or node-target pair were embedded with BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 and calibrated against 166,972 pre-2023 PubMed references using mean top-20 cosine distance. Positive recombination occurred in 8.63% of motifs and had negligible effect on global ranking, whereas specificity and support/GNN reliability terms changed clinical-priority ordering. Robustness analyses across neighbor counts, templates, encoders, generic-label taxonomies, score settings, PrimeKG, and corrected density-based RND showed that broad ordering was more stable than hard top-k membership. A semantic-dose analysis did not support a monotonic relation between score and forecasting benefit after endpoint and token-count adjustment (1.96 days per SD; 95% CI, -0.75 to 4.68). In the frozen catalog-q90 high-semantic subgroup, branch-enhanced forecasting reduced conditional event-time MAE by 20.1 days (95% CI, 13.3-27.0) and sMAPE by 2.37 percentage points (95% CI, 1.81-2.93), while discrimination and endpoint-ranking differences were inconclusive. Corrected RND showed low tail agreement with the primary score (Spearman rho = 0.430; q90 Jaccard = 0.125) despite a similar aggregate timing association. These findings support representation-aware, uncertainty-aware literature-relative prioritization of discovered trajectories rather than causal discovery or clinician-adjudicated novelty.

title: Graph-Enhanced Disease Trajectory Discovery and Temporal Endpoint Forecasting from Longitudinal Electronic Health Records
summary: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) can reveal disease-progression structure, while useful forecasting requires leakage-controlled discovery, censor-aware outcomes, and inspectable trajectory evidence. We developed a graph-enhanced framework in MIMIC-IV v3.1 that splits patients before graph construction, learns train-only consecutive-admission transitions, and freezes endpoint-specific branching-motif policies selected on validation data. The final catalog contained 99,527 motifs, and a time-aware Transformer retrieved at most 24 patient-compatible motifs per endpoint through endpoint-specific cross-attention. Across five training seeds, micro-AUPRC increased from 0.9330 to 0.9357, while event-time MAE decreased from 676.9 to 657.7 days (reduction 19.2 days; 95% paired patient-cluster bootstrap CI, 13.8-24.8). Timing effects were heterogeneous: MAE worsened for events within 730 days but improved by 58.9 days for events occurring after 730 days. In an exploratory internal temporal split, branch conditioning reduced conditional event-time MAE by 26.9 days (95% CI, 23.0-30.8) without evidence of better micro-AUPRC. Corrected survival evaluation over the supported 0-2,555-day interval did not establish macro C-index or integrated Brier score superiority over a matched history-only discrete-hazard model. A directed, degree-matched GNN repair substantially improved unseen-edge discovery, yet replacing GNN-derived scores within fixed motif identities did not improve downstream forecasting. These results position branching motifs as structured trajectory context whose main value is long-range timing support rather than uniformly stronger endpoint discrimination, survival prediction, or causal explanation.

title: Average-Reward Policy Identification from a Single Continuing Trajectory
summary: In reinforcement learning, an agent must explore an unknown environment to learn how to make good decisions. Unlike methods that can freely sample any state--action pair, an agent learning from a single trajectory must spend additional time navigating between states. It is therefore natural to expect that learning from a single trajectory requires more experience. In this paper, we show that this additional cost is not always necessary. For average-reward reinforcement learning, we develop an algorithm that learns where to collect information while ensuring that the required samples can be obtained efficiently. We establish an upper bound on the number of interactions needed to identify a near-optimal policy. Furthermore, we prove a matching information theoretic lower bound, showing that, for a broad class of environments and at sufficiently high accuracy, learning from a single trajectory is no harder in the worst case than learning with unrestricted access to state action samples. Our results reveal that the additional complexity cost of navigation can be avoided by adapting information gathering requirements to how the environment provides information.

title: Decoupled Marginal Sharpening for Training-Free Inference-Time Scaling
summary: We study how to improve LLM reasoning at inference time without updating model weights or using external reward models. Recent reward-free power-sampling methods define the sequence-level power target $\pi_\alpha(y\mid x)\propto p_0(y\mid x)^\alpha$, where $\alpha>1$, which increases the relative probability of completions that are already likely under the base model. Existing methods use Metropolis--Hastings or Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to approximately sample from this target. However, two challenges arise at different levels. At the target level, full-sequence sharpening can concentrate probability on a few exact reasoning--answer trajectories, suppressing alternative paths that support the same answer. At the sampler level, finite-particle SMC can suffer from path collapse when resampling repeatedly duplicates a few high-weight prefixes. To address these challenges, we propose Decoupled Marginal Sharpening (DMS), which separately controls how strongly the model favors particular reasoning paths and how strongly it favors final answers after aggregating support across those paths. At the target level, DMS first samples from a sharpened reasoning distribution, then marginalizes the model's answer probabilities over the resulting weighted reasoning population and sharpens the induced answer marginal. Separate exponents allow mild reasoning sharpening to encourage exploration of diverse paths, followed by stronger answer-marginal sharpening to concentrate probability on answers with greater aggregate support across those paths. At the sampler level, we develop Fully Adapted Annealed SMC, which combines an annealed sequence of power targets with locally fully adapted proposals and predictive ancestor resampling. Experiments on MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, HumanEval, and AIME24/25 across three base models show that DMS achieves the highest mean pass@1 among the compared methods in all tasks.

title: Learning by Examples: Power Grid Steady State Analysis with a Tabular Foundation Model
summary: Foundation models have shown strong generalization across scientific domains, but their use in power systems remains largely task-specific. We investigate whether a pretrained tabular foundation model (TFM), TabPFN, can serve as a general-purpose neural solver for power grid steady-state analysis. We evaluate the TFM on three tasks: power flow (PF) prediction, N-k contingency screening (NCS), and voltage stability margin (VSM) prediction. We performed experiments on 118- and 2000-bus systems, comparing the TFM against task-specific neural baselines. Without retraining or fine-tuning, the TFM matches or outperforms the best task-specific model in several settings across the three tasks. For 118-bus PF prediction, a variant of the TFM achieves errors of $1\times 10^{-3}$ pu for voltage magnitudes and $0.30^\circ$ for voltage angles, outperforming all baselines. On unseen N-1 contingency and close-to-infeasible PF cases, the TFM is competitive with the DCPF approximation. For millions of unseen N-2 contingencies, the TFM achieves AUCs of 0.92 and 0.95 for branch and voltage violation screening, respectively. The TFM also attains accurate VSM prediction performance for the 2000-bus system with limited labelled data. The TFM attains strong results across the tested tasks despite pretraining without any power-system-specific dataset and requiring no fine-tuning step. These results offer a glimpse into the potential of pretrained TFMs as a neural solver for a range of power grid analysis tasks.

title: The Accuracy Well: Nonmonotone Accuracy Dynamics at Vanishing Initialization
comment: 124 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to ICLR-2027: this https URL
summary: We study classification dynamics under small initialization and identify a pronounced non-monotone behavior of accuracy that we call the accuracy well: accuracy rises rapidly early in training, subsequently drops, and only much later recovers. We observe this phenomenon in deep linear networks, fully connected ReLU networks on MNIST, deep convolutional networks on CIFAR-10, and controlled synthetic tasks, across different losses and optimizers and in both training and test accuracy. We propose a three-stage explanation in terms of target-driven organization, a degeneracy bottleneck, and subsequent recruitment and recovery. We develop a rigorous theory of these dynamics for shallow and deep linear networks, showing in particular that high accuracy can emerge while the predictor and the change in loss remain asymptotically vanishing, before continued optimization causes accuracy to deteriorate. For a simple synthetic classification task, we prove an extreme instance in which accuracy asymptotically rises to 100%, collapses to 0, and later recovers permanently to 100%. Our results show that classification accuracy can reveal aspects of learning dynamics that are not captured by the training loss alone.

title: Continual Learning for Reliable In-Sequence Molecular Communication
