summary: Speculative decoding's effectiveness is governed by two quantities: the acceptance rate of drafted tokens and the cost of producing them. We show the two objectives can be co-optimized with algorithm-system co-design, and present JetSpec++, which retains a strong learned draft model while hiding its cost almost entirely. JetSpec++ combines three components: intra-block self refinement, which trains the draft model to iteratively correct its own parallel predictions within a block of tokens; inter-block foresight drafting, which begins the next block before the current one is verified; and pipelined drafting and verification, which overlaps the two stages so drafting's marginal wall-clock cost approaches zero. In comparison with state-of-the-art speculative decoding methods, JetSpec++ attains a wall-clock speedup of up to $7.45\times$ over autoregressive (AR) decoding and $1.54\times$ over DSpark, with up to 1,361 tokens per second for a single request on GB200, and an average acceptance length of 8.94 across seven benchmarks, while preserving the target model's output distribution. Our code and models are available at this https URL .

title: Likelihood Is Not Authorship: Can We Reliably Measure Human Contribution in AI-Assisted Writing?
summary: AI-text detection generally asks whether a machine wrote a text. As AI becomes an increasingly integral and accepted part of writing, the more relevant question is no longer whether AI was used, but how much of the text reflects human contribution. A prominent line of work estimates this by measuring how predictive a person's prompt is of the final text. We show that this measure can be easily manipulated. We introduce SPECIFICITY PADDING that simply asks the model to copy a few random IDs from the prompt, and that alone makes a title-only request look more human than one that supplies the article's key ideas. A context-swap audit then holds each document fixed, and only shows or hides the IDs to the evaluator. The score of the unchanged text swings by a third to half of its scale, and it rises for every document we test, on news and scientific abstracts, across varied LLMs from 3.8B to 753B parameters. The same articles can average 85\% human or 15\% human depending only on which prompt is on record, and even with no prompt at all, the output-only variant rewards the random strings themselves. An exact identity, the credit ledger, explains why. The score is a surprisal-weighted average over the text, so rare strings that the context makes copyable collect the credit, whatever they mean. A two-point bound marks a deeper limit. If the prompt could have been machine-written, every transcript-only method must, in the worst case, miss by half the contribution at stake. Likelihood-based scores alone cannot reliably establish human contribution without evidence of what the person added and how the text was produced.

title: Qwen-MT-Lumen at WMT2026: Instruction-Specialized Translation via Quality-Aware Training and On-Policy Distillation
summary: We present Lumen, The open-source model is available at, our submission to the WMT 2026 General Machine Translation Shared Task. We focus on instruction-specialized translation, where systems must produce accurate translations while satisfying fine-grained requirements on style, terminology, and structured output. Lumen follows a four-stage pipeline. First, continued pre-training and supervised fine-tuning jointly strengthen multilingual translation competence and the ability to follow translation-specific instructions, such as terminology, style, and format constraints. Second, we extend the originally offline M^{2}PO preference-optimization framework into an online preference-optimization stage: the current policy samples candidate translations, an LLM judge assigns continuous direct-assessment scores, and the resulting multi-pair preferences are used to update the model. Third, on-policy distillation transfers stronger translation-instruction-following behavior from a larger teacher model to the Qwen3-14B student, improving translation-instruction adherence while retaining a 14B primary translation backbone. Finally, structure-aware inference and postprocessing preserve required formats, while selective repair addresses clear structural or decoding failures before submission. We participate in 23 translation directions. Under an absolute 1--5 LLM-judge rubric that evaluates translation-instruction following and translation quality separately, Lumen reaches an overall mean score of 4.60. Despite using a 14B translation backbone, it achieves performance comparable to leading proprietary systems in both translation quality and translation-instruction following.

title: Beyond Reachability: A Relation-Semantic Reasoning Framework for Biomedical Multi-hop QA
summary: Biomedical multi-hop reasoning over knowledge graphs requires identifying a semantically valid relation sequence that supports the answer. Existing methods can retrieve correct answers, yet often rank them poorly within a large pool of seemingly relevant candidates. Even when a correct answer is retrieved, its associated evidence and reasoning path may fail to support the relation composition required by the question. We term this disconnect between answer reachability and evidential validity the reachable-but-invalid problem. We present ReSemReason, which shares a question-induced distribution over typed, directed relation schemas between candidate discovery and evidence selection. Schema compatibility guides graph search; ReSemAttn then uses relation-conditioned key/value projections and an uncertainty-weighted path prior to attend to candidate-specific evidence. A separate absolute-support score complements normalized attention when all retrieved paths are weak. The reported experiments on BioHopR, PrimeKGQA, and MedReason show improvements in answer ranking and answer-set quality. Path-discrimination analyses examine the distinction between endpoint correctness and evidential support. We also specify matched controls for search, attention, and schema uncertainty.

title: MakSafe: A Spatiotemporal Semantic Framework for Formal Specification and Compliance Checking of Road Vehicle Safety Rules
summary: Scenario-based validation is essential for automated road vehicles but cannot cover the full variability of openworld traffic. We present MakSafe, a formal spatiotemporal framework for specifying and checking road vehicle safety rules through semantic zones, action-based forecasting, and trace-tree reasoning, avoiding uniform time discretization. We formalize the road network, vehicle states, and occupancy zones, then build executable rules for front-vehicle identification and timeto-collision (TTC) verification. The evaluation combines a tracedependent case study with a scalability benchmark over traffic density (N ), horizon (H), and branch factor (B). MakSafe yields branch-specific verdicts, deriving safe and unsafe outcomes from the same initial scene, and re-evaluates a scenario after a control update. A single rule check stays well below a millisecond across the reported sweep, and longer horizons slow the TTC check.

title: Beyond State Capacity: Why Retrieval Breaks in Mamba
summary: Mamba models underperform Transformers on in-context retrieval. This gap is usually attributed to Mamba's fixed-size recurrent state, which loses information as the context grows. We challenge this assumption by focusing on query-first retrieval, a setup in which the query precedes the context and state capacity should not be the binding constraint. We show that even in this setting Mamba lags substantially behind Transformers, despite its selection mechanism, which was designed to distinguish relevant content from distractors. We then demonstrate that the Mamba selection gates have sufficient control over the state updates to influence the model output: intervening on specific gates alone can swing accuracy between extremes. However, as gates are input-dependent, they require the incoming token's representation to encode its relevance to the query. We therefore probe token representations across layers, and find that the relevance signal emerges only gradually with model depth, and that the gates begin to reflect it only several layers deeper. Crucially, we find that gates in retrieval-critical layers are not yet aligned with relevance. The selection mechanism is thus expressive enough to solve the task, but it commonly operates on a relevance signal that has not yet arrived. Mamba's retrieval bottleneck therefore extends beyond state capacity: even when capacity is sufficient, the delayed emergence of relevance information across depth often prevents successful retrieval.

title: RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing
summary: LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.

title: BANGLAPLAN: A Benchmark for Constraint-Based Planning and Decision-Making in Bangla
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly help users arrange appointments, plan journeys, and allocate limited resources. These tasks require models to satisfy constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, or determine that no feasible solution exists. Bangla is the world's seventh most widely spoken language, and existing benchmarks cover many language and reasoning tasks. However, benchmarks for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla under explicit constraints remain lacking. We introduce BANGLAPLAN, a benchmark of 1,000 problems across ten task families grounded in everyday life and institutions in Bangladesh. It includes feasible and infeasible problems in four language registers: everyday, formal, colloquial, and Bangla--English mixed. Answers cover eight structured types, including schedules, routes, allocations, and ordered steps, in a common JSON format. We construct the benchmark through language-model-assisted drafting and independent human validation. We evaluate 11 open-weight and proprietary model configurations using exact match, separately reporting feasible-case accuracy, infeasibility detection, and format errors. We find a large performance gap: GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 98.7% accuracy and Qwen3.5-27B with thinking reaches 80.3%, while direct-answer configurations score at most 30.9%. Seven of eleven configurations perform below the always-``infeasible'' baseline. Our findings also suggest that harder problems primarily reduce plan-construction accuracy, while infeasibility detection remains more robust. BANGLAPLAN provides a reproducible basis for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla. BANGLAPLAN is available at: this https URL .

title: Share the Symbol, Not the Vector: Training-Free Fact Communication Across Language Models
comment: Project page: this https URL Code: this https URL Data: this https URL
summary: Multi-agent systems allow language models to solve tasks collaboratively by sharing complementary information. These systems typically communicate through text, while recent approaches also explore exchanging internal model states. However, sharing these states across architectures often requires learned translators or assumptions about model compatibility. We introduce SYNC (Symbol-Indexed Neural Communication), a word-indexed interface that connects heterogeneous models without fine-tuning or a learned translator. From descriptions only it can see, the sender selects words from a shared list and sends their indices for each object, without seeing the questions. The receiver writes the described facts into its hidden states using its own word directions, vectors fitted once from its activations. We test selective use by swapping one attribute between two objects and requiring correct answers about both changed and unchanged attributes before and after the swap, four answers in total. We choose an early write layer on four development receivers and then fix it. With three different senders and nine newer receivers from five families, four-answer success on new scenes reaches 72.0-98.3%, up to 96 percentage points above middle-layer writing, and the two largest receivers match plain text. A task-free probe predicted in advance which depths each new receiver can use (45 of 45 cases). Without retuning, messages listing every fact keep 89.6-100% success under new layouts, and sender messages reach 23.9-64.0% on a landmark task with multi-token symbols, below text but from 0% without a message. These results show that shared word indices and receiver-local directions can support selective fact use across model families without additional training.

title: Selective Reasoning for Typed Decision Models: When to Start, Read, and Stop
comment: 24 pages, 4 figures. Both authors contributed equally. Code and evaluation materials: this https URL
summary: Typed decision models need an interface that can use additional reasoning while retaining candidate outputs. We train a shared candidate-answer reader on a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone to unify direct decisions with on-demand, interruptible reasoning. The reader returns distributions from empty and partial reasoning prefixes. A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests explicit reads, and an entropy rule accepts acquired answers and cancels generation. Measurements distinguish answer-query work, generated output, and pipeline time. Across 768 questions from ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge, accuracy rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%. Relative to 512-token terminal reading, accuracy improves by 7.29 percentage points with 2.25% more mean output work. Relative to 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time falls by 46.30% with an accuracy difference of -1.17 points. Exact-prefix controls isolate the saving from interruption, while read-scheduling controls distinguish reduced observation work from shorter response time.

title: J-tau: A Fully Localized Japanese Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction
summary: We present J-tau, the first publicly available Japanese benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents in interactive customer-support scenarios. While tau-bench is widely used to evaluate LLM agents, it is English-centric and cannot evaluate agents in other languages. Existing multilingual extensions offer no public Japanese version and rely primarily on machine translation, leaving locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies inconsistent with the target region. To enable reliable evaluation in Japanese, we carefully localize tau-bench through machine translation, entity adaptation, and human review. During this process, we also uncover and fix two flaws in the original tau-bench: invalid tasks and a score aggregation error that inflates certain models' results. Experiments show that J-tau yields fewer evaluation errors than a naively machine-translated counterpart and that our fixes resolve both flaws.

title: Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs
summary: As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design.

title: PA1-OPD: One-Step Prefix-Augmented On-Policy Distillation for Language Model Pretraining
summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) improves language-model pretraining by matching teacher distributions at corpus prefixes, but provides no direct supervision at contexts induced by student predictions. We introduce PA1-OPD, which augments corpus-path distillation with teacher feedback after one student-sampled transition per selected prefix. This expands the supervised states while retaining next-token prediction and corpus-path KD. Data-anchored roots support parallel sampling, and differentiable tree attention shares prefix computation without changing inference. In two continued-pretraining settings, full coverage improves held-out cross-entropy over KD across C4, PG-19, and Pile at every evaluated checkpoint. In Stage2, selecting the 10% of roots with highest student surprisal adds 48.85% to KD's Macro cross-entropy gain over next-token training. Gains remain when branch supervision excludes successor states already on the corpus path, supporting the value of feedback beyond observed contexts. Additional depth or breadth improves aggregate results at unchanged per-term supervision weight, with benefits varying by corpus. These findings support local student-induced supervision as a complement to pretraining distillation.

title: Moral Combat: Exploiting Moral Foundations Theory to Jailbreak LLMs
summary: Social psychology has long described how people can be persuaded to interpret a harmful act as moral. Recent research suggests that Large Language Models (LLMs) echo aspects of human psychology, from cognitive biases to social conformity. This raises a question with direct safety implications: can LLMs be moralized to bypass safety guardrails? We answer this question with a multi-agent framework grounded in Moral Foundations Theory (MFT). Given a harmful request that is initially refused, our agents diagnose which moral foundation (MF) the prompt is violating, identify a justifiable foundation under which the same request appears virtuous, rewrite the prompt accordingly, and reinforce it with generated precedents of comparable moral reframing. We evaluate our framework on harmful prompts from three well-known jailbreak datasets across five open-source and proprietary models. Our analysis reveals that models are highly susceptible to moralization, exhibiting high single-trial jailbreak rates with success increasing further under repeated attempts. We also find that safety benchmarks are imbalanced in the MFs they violate, concentrating on foundations toward which models already exhibit biases.

title: GraphRAG-LTM: A Layered Threat Modeling Framework for Attacks on Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) uses document-derived knowledge graphs to assemble evidence for large language model (LLM) answers. Its security depends on both the seed chunks retrieved for a query and the graph evidence assembled from them, yet attacks on this evidence path remain underexplored. We introduce GraphRAG-LTM, a Layered Threat Modeling framework that tests three nested levels of attacker access. BB Query uses ranking feedback to make query edits under a semantic-similarity constraint and demote relevant seed chunks. WB Query uses retriever gradients for the same objective. Graph-aware WB keeps the white-box adversarial query and deletes bridge triplets from the query-specific evidence graph, disrupting multi-hop evidence propagation through localized graph edits. Across datasets, retrievers, and LLM backbones, rank feedback alone reduces answer quality, gradient access strengthens query attacks, and bridge-triplet deletion further impairs supporting-fact retrieval. Further analyses show how seed retrieval and graph evidence jointly contribute to these failures.

title: One Block Ahead: Promoting Sampler State in Diffusion Language Models
summary: Block-diffusion language models denoise a whole block of token positions in parallel so each forward pass can emit many tokens. However, blocks are still denoised in strict sequence, a cost that within-block acceleration leaves untouched. Here, we investigate decoding blocks concurrently and propose One Block Ahead (OBA), a training-free decoding algorithm that denoises the next block alongside the current one. We demonstrate that for uniform-state diffusion LMs, where a block's denoising progress is not visible in its intermediate tokens, concurrent decoding is advantageous if the next block's tokens are promoted together with the corresponding sampler state, including the self-conditioning signal and the denoising time. We also derive a break-even criterion that relates the benefit of OBA to the relative cost of a paired-block forward pass. On DiffusionGemma, a state-of-the-art diffusion LM, OBA increases the tokens per forward pass by 42.3% (from 15.64 to 22.25) and the single-request denoising throughput by 16.3%, averaged over ten benchmarks, with a small accuracy regression.

title: Towards Efficient Simultaneous Inverse Text Normalization with Pretrained Text-to-Text Language Model and Read-Tag-Write Policy
summary: Streaming Inverse Text Normalization (ITN) is vital for converting spoken-form outputs from streaming Automatic Speech Recognition into formatted written text. Existing streaming ITN methods rely on hybrid systems combining neural tagging with expert-crafted finite-state transducer rules, limiting scalability across domains and languages. While end-to-end models offer superior scalability by learning directly from data, standard encoder-decoder architectures are inherently non-streaming due to global attention. In this paper, we propose an efficient streaming end-to-end ITN system, adapting a pretrained text-to-text model to leverage its robust linguistic knowledge. To enable streaming, we introduce architectural adaptations, a specialized training strategy, a Read-Tag-Write decoding policy, and inference optimizations. Experiments on Vietnamese datasets show accuracy comparable to non-streaming baselines, outperforming hybrid methods while satisfying real-time latency requirements.

title: AgriJev: Efficient Agricultural Candidate Scoring with Multi-Scale Adapted Models
summary: Agricultural systems make decisions over heterogeneous entity types, textual judgments, and knowledge-question options. Generating a textual answer adds decoding and extraction steps to decisions that ultimately require a candidate choice. We introduce AgriJev, a family of adapted Qwen3.5 models at 0.8B, 2B, 4B, and 9B. A shared interface conditions on agricultural text, a judgment question, and candidate definitions, returning scores and relative probabilities in one forward call. We prepare source-aware training records and frozen evaluations from existing agricultural resources, retaining original groups and annotation provenance. Comparisons include original Qwen3.5 models and matched agricultural SFT models, both evaluated through native answer generation. Across 17 external test views, AgriJev-9B reaches 75.44% mean accuracy, exceeding the original and SFT generators by 5.89 and 3.79 percentage points. It outperforms the original generator on 13 views and narrows the mean gap to hosted Jev 1.13.0. On a fixed A100 workload, its median scoring latency is approximately half that of same-scale answer generation. Task-dependent gains and failures characterize a practical choice among agricultural model weights and inference contracts.

title: More Than Seeing: Vision as Scalable Anchors in Native Multimodal Pre-Training
summary: Native multimodal pre-training trains a single model from scratch on text and multimodal data, enabling it to understand both language and visual inputs. However, how visual signals shape scaling behavior and support capabilities beyond visual understanding remains unclear. We investigate this question through controlled visual-content ablations across model sizes and training budgets. Specifically, we replace image embeddings with content-free padding token embeddings. Retaining visual content improves text prediction on image-text examples without materially changing the lowest text-only loss at a given compute budget, the optimal balance of model size and training data, or aggregate language scores. The relative multimodal loss benefit grows approximately as a power law of compute. To test benefits beyond understanding images, we evaluate spatial reasoning from text descriptions alone. Both conditions improve with model and data scaling. During training of the largest model, visual gains are most sustained in localization, navigation, and symbolic planning, which involve maintaining object configurations or composing spatial updates; gains in spatial relations, geometry, and physical commonsense are less consistent. These findings identify visual content as a scalable anchor for multimodal learning, with benefits that extend beyond visual inputs while preserving aggregate language performance.

title: ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures. The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a $2.49\times$ training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.

title: The Sum of All Summaries: PROPALIGN for Graded Proposition Salience Evaluation
summary: Identification and ranking of salient propositions in documents is indirectly involved in many AI tasks, but few papers define proposition salience scores clearly, make diverse data available, or evaluate models directly on the task. This paper proposes PROPALIGN, a multiple-summary-based approach for propositional salience score estimation, and releases PROPALIGNBANK, an accompanying dataset for the method with 138K alignments of over 35K propositions. We compare several approaches to salient proposition extraction in English across a broad range of spoken and written genres, and demonstrate that naively asking models for judgments leads to inconsistencies. By contrast, graded, summary-based metrics are more stable. We further observe that while single models perform worse than humans, an ensemble of models incorporating linguistic features approaches manual annotation quality ceilings. In addition, analyses of the model outputs suggest insights into how models can extract salient information with and without the use of summaries.

title: Learning What to Keep: Transfer-Aware Personal Skill Learning from User Feedback
summary: User feedback enables LLMs to refine reusable personalized skills, but often mixes persistent preferences with request-specific corrections. Indiscriminately retaining both risks negative transfer, motivating selective retention at the level of individual requirements. We frame this challenge as selective transfer over atomic rules and propose SkillGrain, a framework for learning reusable personalized skills from user feedback. SkillGrain decomposes feedback into independently actionable rules, predicts their transferability, and retains only those suitable for future requests. To learn these decisions, we combine rubric-guided skill rewards with fine-grained credit assignment that separately evaluates rule content and retention decisions. We further jointly optimize skill induction and skill-conditioned generation through reinforcement learning, ensuring that learned skills support downstream personalization. We construct a benchmark spanning five personalized writing tasks to evaluate cross-request generalization. Experiments across three base models in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings show that SkillGrain achieves the best overall average performance among competing methods.

title: PersEvalBench: Can LLM Evaluators Judge Contextually Appropriate Use of Persona Information?
summary: Large language model (LLM) evaluators are increasingly used to assess personalized assistants, yet whether they can reliably judge personalization has rarely been tested. We introduce PersEvalBench, a benchmark testing whether an evaluator can recognize appropriate and inappropriate uses of user history. It contains 403 multi-episode scenarios where user information should persist, transfer, or cease to apply. The benchmark covers nine controlled error subtypes across three families: under-personalization, over-personalization, and misapplied-state errors. Human audits confirm that generated errors match their intended types and that the prescribed uses of user information are reasonable. Across five LLM evaluators, recognition of controlled personalization errors remains limited even with the full dialogue history. On the human-evaluated subset, under-personalization shows the largest gap: humans recognize 94.4% of these errors, compared with 63.9% for the strongest reported evaluator. Evaluators often recognize that a response is problematic but reverse the error direction, mistaking failure to follow an applicable preference (UNDER) for use of an inapplicable preference (OVER). Easier evidence access offers little help: highlighting the relevant history turns raises error recognition only slightly, suggesting that the remaining difficulty lies in judging what role that information should play in the response.

title: Qwenfant: Train Big Character-level BabyLMs on Concise Parallel Text
summary: This work concerns our submission for the Multilingual track of the 2026 BabyLM Challenge. We improve on our baseline using data that has been summarized and translated by an LLM, showing that higher-quality data can come from synthetic sources. We further improve with 2 simple changes: using a larger model, and using a character-level vocabulary. Both of these changes require LoRA-style fine-tuning for realizing their full potential. We dub our final Qwen3-based model Qwenfant, which, at the time of submission, ranks 1st in the Multilingual track.

title: Can LLM Agents Efficiently Identify Appliance Faults? Insights From Diagnosing a Simulated Appliance
summary: In so-called "Industry 4.0," integrated sensors, analytics tools, and other digital technologies supplement industrial workflows, potentiating enhanced visibility and automation. Prognostics and health management (PHM) and natural language processing (NLP) practitioners alike have explored the application of large language models (LLMs) to industrial asset management, but many prior works' focus on exam-like benchmarks has limited their assessment of LLMs' ability to automate practical operations. Herein, we introduce CoffeeBench, a fault diagnostics task for LLM agents, using a simulated appliance. The LLMs we evaluate struggle to consistently identify faults from the sensor information alone, but the best-performing ones can iteratively refine the fault-option space to eventually obtain a successful diagnosis. Our subsequent analyses, therefore, focus on: differentiating models by diagnostic efficiency (RQ1); examining the lagging performance of the three worst models (RQ2); and identifying viable heuristics for selective prediction (RQ3), including that initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning are high-signal predictors of diagnostic success. In addition to our benchmark results (Section 3.1), we provide practical insights for improving the performance of the open-weight models on CoffeeBench, such as by explicitly tracking episode state on their behalf to reduce timeouts (Section 3.2) or applying a deliberation loop to refine diagnostic hypotheses (Section 3.3).

title: DUALVIEW: Leveraging Broad and Output-Specific Evidence for LLM-based Multi-Output Text Regression
summary: While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. \method{} first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.

title: Weighted Ensemble Sampling for Rare-Event Estimation in Language Models
summary: Rare but severe failures of large language models can become practically significant at deployment scale. Estimating their probabilities with direct Monte Carlo sampling is highly inefficient, while proposal-based methods typically require auxiliary learning of an additional proposal distribution. We introduce \textbf{Weighted Ensemble (WE)}, a training-free framework for rare-event estimation in language models. WE samples exclusively from the original language model and improves upon direct Monte Carlo by periodically reallocating the sampling budget toward prefixes that appear more likely to reach the target rare event. To guide this reallocation without learning a separate proposal distribution, we exploit internal LLM representations as prefix-level signals and empirically validate their effectiveness. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on safety-related tasks spanning both small-scale and modern large-scale LLMs demonstrate that WE improves the efficiency and reliability of rare-event probability estimation.

title: NEPSEE: A Double-Annotated Benchmark for Nepali Sentiment Analysis
summary: Many sentiment datasets use one annotator for each item, so the test labels show the conventions of that person. We build a Nepali benchmark from two annotators who labelled the same sentences blind. They labelled 5,614 sentences from tweets of Nepali public figures on a five-point scale. We keep only the 3,189 sentences where both give the same polarity. On the three-class benchmark, NepBERTa with a fixed tokenizer gets a macro-F1 of 0.877 and IndicBERTv2 0.867. Three commercial large language models (LLMs) get 0.882 to 0.896 zero-shot, and these differences are not significant. On the five-point scale, 766 sentences have two adjacent labels, for example Pos and SPos. We accept both labels and train on both. On this task, Claude Opus 5.5 beats the best encoders by 0.10 to 0.12 macro-F1. A tokenizer audit adds a second result. The default tokenizers of three Nepali BERT models delete the non-spacing Devanagari vowel signs and the virama. When we restore the marks, macro-F1 increases by 0.084 for NepBERTa but decreases by 0.095 for a model pretrained on stripped text.

title: How to Evaluate When You Don't Know How to Evaluate? Choosing Reliable Setups for Base Language Model Benchmarking
summary: Evaluation of large language models (LLMs) remains largely pre-scientific: it involves many design decisions, with little guidance on how to make them. These choices can substantially affect measured performance and, consequently, decisions about subsequent pretraining. To identify effective evaluation setups, we investigate 8 aspects, such as task formulation or the number of in-context examples. We compare the setups using three widely-used signal criteria, repurposed as normative meta-measures: monotonicity, non-randomness, and ranking consistency of the evaluation scores across intermediate checkpoints. In an early pretraining scenario, we evaluate these setups on 26 monolingual 2B-parameter models trained on different types of data, using 80 tasks in four languages. We also examine the setups on three larger LLMs ($\geq$7B) in the same four languages and explore how the preferred setups change with model scale. Our results yield concrete recommendations: some choices, such as the use of multiple prompts, are consistently useful, whereas others, such as task formulation, depend on model scale. More generally, our framework serves as a recipe for the choice of evaluation setups in new scenarios.

title: HERO: Harnessing Evidence for Test-time Refinement and Prompt Optimization in Program Generation
summary: Harness optimization improves LLMs by refining reusable prompts and scaffolding, yet requires further adaptation for program generation tasks such as text-to-SQL and text-to-Python. Existing methods often rely on LLM reflectors to propose harness updates, which can fix observed failures but also disrupt previously correct behavior. Text-to-code tasks offer a natural way to mitigate this issue: we can execute generated outputs, allowing us to evaluate and verify the effects of proposed updates directly. Building on this signal, we introduce \textsc{HERO} (\textbf{H}arnessing \textbf{E}vidence for \textbf{R}efinement and \textbf{O}ptimization), which combines offline and test-time harness optimization. At the first stage, \method{} learns reusable prompt updates from execution-verified successes and failures and validates candidate revisions before adoption. At test time, we treat the generated code as an instance-specific harness and refine it using execution feedback. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, \method{} achieves the best offline performance, improving pass@1 by \(7.6\) points over the initial prompt, while test-time refinement adds another \(2.0\) points and improves execution efficiency.

title: Fantastic Metrics and How to Find Them: Meta-Evaluating Metrics for Multi-lingual Style-Personalized Generation
summary: Meta-evaluation of text generation metrics and LLM-judges is primarily conducted using metric-human correlations. However, prior work has shown that correlation is not an appropriate estimate of a metric's evaluation capability and can be unstable across evaluation settings, such as different datasets or languages. Therefore, we propose a regression-based meta-evaluation of metrics that learns on calibrated metric outputs to predict human ratings. We ground this measurement relative to a trivial constant-mean baseline and human agreements to provide a comparable measure of metric capability across evaluation settings. To test our meta-evaluation framework, we developed a large-scale multi-lingual style-personalized text generation (SPTG) benchmark, collecting multiple annotations across 10 topologically diverse languages and four evaluation dimensions, each with varying degrees of subjectivity. We meta-evaluated 32 metrics from three style evaluation paradigms (string-based, embedding-based, and LLM-judges) and their ensembles over these 40 evaluation settings. Our analysis revealed that even simple string- and embedding-based measurements can match strong LLM-judges when calibrated to human ratings. We also identified characteristics of human annotations that determine metric performance, as well as conditions under which a metric ensemble outperforms its individual constituents.

title: From Qualitative Text to Integrated Evidence: The Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI) Procedure
comment: 23 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Code available at this https URL
summary: Mixed methods research offers established strategies for integrating qualitative and quantitative evidence, but less guidance for integrating two computational representations of the same qualitative corpus. This methodological study introduces Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI), a four-step procedure for explicit and traceable integration. We present PTI using 1,203 interview paragraphs from 29 mothers in Nepal. The two representations were ontology-guided Patient Voice (PV) coding with PVminer and data-driven themes generated through non-negative matrix factorization (NMF). A theme-complete crosswalk documented convergence, divergence, and preprocessing-sensitive differences. Depression status, based on Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scores, served as a secondary external anchor for exploratory association checks. PTI provides a structured approach for integrating computational representations of qualitative text within mixed methods research.

title: DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures, including references and appendices. Benchmark website: this https URL
summary: Emerging decision models such as JEV provide typed interfaces that map task instructions and observations directly to choices, judgments, and scores. As these models are increasingly used for automated decision-making, understanding their reliability under adversarial manipulation becomes critical. We introduce DecisionRobust, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of decision models across textual and visual inputs. Our benchmark covers practical decision-making scenarios and a diverse suite of attacks, including semantics-preserving text perturbations, image perturbations, and prompt injection in both modalities. We curate evaluation sets through external validity checks and cross-model candidate selection. We evaluate 30 model configurations on text tasks and 17 on vision tasks, including 24 and 12 held-out models, respectively, that are excluded from candidate selection. Our experiments reveal several key findings. First, attacks expose vulnerabilities beyond the models used for construction and selection, although optimized image perturbations transfer weakly to many targets even with multiple surrogates. Second, relative model robustness varies across tasks and attack types, and resistance to input perturbations does not necessarily imply resistance to prompt injection. Third, label-consistency checks substantially reduce measured attack success across text and image settings, highlighting the importance of validating apparent failures. The benchmark is available at this https URL .

title: Pre-Trained Language Models as Zero-Shot Tools for Social Science Research
summary: Record linkage and demographic inference from names are routine demands in social science. Most approaches to these problems require labeled training data that are difficult or costly to acquire. I show that pre-trained language models perform both tasks accurately without requiring task-specific training. For record linkage, I introduce EnsembleLink, an algorithm that uses pre-trained embeddings alongside string-based scorers to retrieve a short list of candidates and then identify the likeliest matches. EnsembleLink matches or exceeds the performance of most prior approaches while generalizing across scripts and formats that those methods are unable to handle. For ethnicity inference from names, I show that large language models (LLMs) achieve up to 83.8% accuracy on U.S. voter files, compared to 78.0% for name-supplemented BISG. Open-weight models offer reproducible implementations that approach these models in accuracy. Moreover, LLMs are able to infer group membership for religious, caste-based, and other ethnic group categories outside of the United States, and reduce bias in downstream estimates of geographic racial gaps. Where pre-training encodes the world knowledge required by each task, task-specific labels add less information.

title: Crossing the Gender Binary: Modelling Gendered Reference in Science Fiction and General Fiction
summary: Science fiction is widely credited with unsettling gender. This article asks whether that holds at the linguistic level, in how readily gendered reference gives way to its counterpart, a neutral term, or other social category, and whether it separates the genre from general fiction. It does so by masking man/men, woman/women, and person/people across same-period science fiction and general fiction corpora and classifying RoBERTa's five likeliest substitutes by gender. Retention and displacement are permutation-tested over five resampling rounds, and the underlying sentences are read closely. Both corpora cross the gender binary in both directions, but unequally: where woman is masked, the model predicts a masculine term about twice as often as it predicts a feminine term where man is masked. Each mismatch marks a statistical surprise, a word the corpus did not expect there. Against this shared pattern, science fiction shows greater gender permeability than the general fiction corpus, placing man in feminine contexts more often than general fiction while the reverse rate holds steady. Its degendering tendency is stronger too, drawing both gendered terms toward the neutral. Beyond the binary, a masked woman also draws substitutes naming a social category and no gender far more often than a masked man does. In measuring the gender permeability of man, woman, and person in linguistic distribution and testing whether genre changes it, the study gives science fiction studies linguistic evidence for thematic claims and computational literary studies a pipeline applicable to other category vocabularies, such as race and class.

title: Joint Subspace Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Decoding
summary: Sparse attention reduces the KV-cache traffic that dominates long-context LLM decoding, but practical methods largely operate at coarse granularity. Token-level selection offers finer control, yet presents two challenges: low-dimensional scoring may lose query--key structure needed for accurate ranking, while gathering scattered selected tokens can offset the resulting latency benefit. We introduce Joint Subspace Sparse Attention (JSSA) to address both challenges. For selection quality, JSSA learns a shared low-dimensional query--key subspace by minimizing token-score preservation error. We upper-bound the resulting non-convex objective with a tractable marginal objective that admits a closed-form spectral solution; direct refinement of the exact objective provides no measurable improvement in the tested settings. For execution efficiency, we develop a gather-free token-level indexed-attention kernel that supports distinct per-KV-head selections under the standard grouped-query attention (GQA) KV-cache layout. Across standard GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global attention, and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) models, JSSA consistently remains close to full-KV accuracy while avoiding the substantial generation-length inflation and architecture-dependent failures observed with competing methods. On an NVIDIA B200 GPU, JSSA achieves up to $6.43\times$ the decoding throughput of full-KV attention at 128K context. JSSA achieves reasoning accuracy comparable to model-native DSA without model training and reaches 96--99\% of its decoding throughput even at 700B scale large models.

title: Can LLMs Access their World Knowledge for Event Prediction?
summary: Recent work has questioned whether large language models (LLMs) can be useful for temporal event prediction. Despite vast pretrained world knowledge, LLMs often underperform simpler specialized models. We ask whether this knowledge is truly inaccessible, or whether current methods fail to present event prediction in a form LLMs can use. We argue for the latter and show that LLMs become effective event forecasters when the interface is designed around two choices. The first grounds each event in a natural-language description, and the second separates event semantics from the prediction space to prevent semantic bias from label associations. To test this, we introduce DescribeEvent, a benchmark of ~150K events across seven datasets and six domains with event-level descriptions. We find that capable LLMs substantially benefit from descriptions and symbolic labels, outperforming description-free variants and non-LLM baselines, while weaker models gain little. These results suggest that accessing LLM world knowledge for event prediction is an interface problem, and that event descriptions offer a practical way to elicit the knowledge LLMs already encode.

title: Twenty Days Later: A Pre-Registered Test of History-Based Forecasts of Brand Mentions in Gemini Answers
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Pre-registered at this https URL . Data: this https URL
summary: Counts of which brands a large language model names are useful only if they hold long enough to act on. We test this with a pre-registered replication. The same 162 requests (54 questions in English, Estonian and Finnish about three software categories, four of twelve candidate brands per question, three repeats) were sent to gemini-3.1-pro-preview in three waves within about ten hours on 22 and 23 September 2026, and again on 13 October 2026, 20.3 days after the third wave, with identical request bodies. The plan and its decision rule were frozen, hashed and registered on OSF before the first call. The outcome is a lexical mention label per answer and brand, 648 per wave. The primary forecast, each brand-and-question cell's mention rate over the nine earlier answers, scored Brier 0.0281 and log loss 0.126, against Brier 0.0259 for the six-answer forecast of the 8-hour wave and a registered ceiling of 0.0559. It beat brand history (0.104), the overall rate (0.234) and a constant 0.5 (0.250) on both scores and in all nine question families (exact sign-flip p = 0.0039), so durability holds under the registered rule. A forecast frozen from the first wave alone scored 0.0599, 0.0587 and 0.0604 at horizons of 1.5 hours, 9.6 hours and 20.7 days. Of the 202 cells unanimous in the 8-hour wave, 194 were unchanged at D1 and none reversed. The latest wave alone was nearly as accurate as the pooled history (Brier 0.0292; pooled lower in 5 of 9 families, p = 0.28). Every answer reported the requested model version, and none issued a search query although search was enabled. A blind human check of 96 labels agreed with the rule on 94; both disagreements were adjudicated as rater omissions, so after adjudication the rule matched on 96 of 96. The test covers one model, one interval and twelve known brands, and estimates no decay rate.

title: From Efficiency to Sufficiency: The Cost-Aware Measurement Design Framework for Automated Essay Scoring
summary: Compute cost in automated essay scoring (AES) is usually treated as a technical efficiency issue rather than a measurement design concern. Yet deployment decisions require more than reporting latency, model size, or inference expense. In high-stakes settings, total burden includes validation, monitoring, adjudication, compliance, and governance; in instructional settings, pricing, licensing, and integration may dominate cost. This paper reframes AES as a cost-constrained measurement system and introduces the Cost-Aware Measurement Design (CAMD) Framework, a four-layer structure consisting of metering, allocation, unit economics, and decision, for translating computational and workflow resource records into decision-relevant cost constructs. Direct cost is specified as monetary outlay plus attributable labor and time, and two criteria, design attribution and auditability, determine what the cost boundary excludes. Burdens that satisfy neither criterion, such as institutional capability and governance posture, are represented as constraints on which designs are admissible rather than priced. The paper defines cost per defensible score (CPDS) and argues that AES systems should be compared by quality-cost sufficiency: minimizing cost among defensible scoring designs that satisfy measurement requirements. Scoring volume conditions all four layers, so cost per defensible score is treated as a function of scale rather than as a single transferable number. CAMD provides a portable basis for representing, comparing, and evaluating cost across AES studies and deployment contexts.

title: Creating SquashFS Images to Support HPC and AI Datasets
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, IEEE High Performance Extreme Computing (HPEC) Conference 2026
summary: HPC users often download datasets on HPC systems for analysis and processing. When these datasets are comprised of hundreds of thousands (or more) of small files, accessing them in parallel can put a tremendous burden on the metadata servers of central parallel file systems. If the dataset is read-only, an effective solution is to compress the dataset into a SquashFS image. There are, however, a number of workflows that can be used to create such a dataset image, and we observed that some were more efficient than others. To provide more effective guidance for our userbase, we benchmarked eleven different workflows for creating SquashFS dataset image files of datasets with thousands to millions of very small files. We took into account whether the data arrived as this http URL , zip, or files-and-directories downloads, whether the image creation was on the central file system or local compute node storage, and the number of SquashFS file compression threads used. This paper shares the results of these benchmarks and provides recommendations to HPC system users toward the best workflows to use for SquashFS image creation.

title: XViewRank: Overlap-Conditioned Score Fusion for LLM-Augmented Sparse Retrieval
summary: Large language models can reduce vocabulary mismatch in sparse retrieval by generating alternative views of a query. Once these views are searched independently, however, their ranked lists may be complementary, redundant, or affected by query drift, making fixed fusion suboptimal. We present XViewRank, a lightweight retrieval-side method for conditionally fusing BM25 results from an original query, a hypothesis view, and a step-back view. For each pooled candidate, XViewRank retains three normalized BM25 scores and three query-level overlaps between the retrieved result sets. A small nonlinear scorer uses the overlaps as context that changes how the view-specific scores are interpreted, without jointly encoding query and passage text. Under a matched-input protocol, XViewRank improves nDCG@10 and MAP numerically over reciprocal rank fusion on both TREC DL 2019 and 2020, with a statistically significant MAP gain on DL19. Additional analyses show that the clearest benefit occurs when the view rankings have low agreement, while the evidence on DL20 is weaker. The results support overlap-conditioned score fusion as a compact retrieval-side alternative to fixed fusion, while also delimiting where its advantage is empirically established.

title: Reading the Neighborhood: Text-Attentive Graph Reranking for Automated Subject Indexing
comment: Presented at the ACM/IEEE-CS Joint Conference on Digital Libraries (JCDL) 2026
summary: Subject indexing assigns descriptors from a controlled vocabulary to bibliographic records, a task characterized by thousands of labels, few positive examples per label, and a long tail of rarely used descriptors. Existing extreme multi-label classifiers treat the vocabulary as a flat list, ignoring the semantic relations that thesauri encode. We present TAGHN, a heterogeneous graph reranker over a per-document subgraph of retrieved candidates augmented with the thesaurus neighborhood. The relevance of a candidate descriptor is estimated jointly from its similarity with the document and also the degree to which the candidate's thesaurus neighborhood matches the document content. A decomposed scoring head combines interpretable graph-derived features with retrieval signals. On STW, an economic thesaurus of 6,198 descriptors, TAGHN reaches 0.380 macro F1 against 0.346 for a fine-tuned cross-encoder and 0.278 for a fixed-vocabulary XMLC classifier. In terms of micro F1, it outperforms reranking models and stays competitive (-3.0) with the best fixed-vocabulary XMLC model. Qualitative analysis shows the graph resolving errors that per-label scoring cannot, selecting a narrower gold descriptor where an unstructured reranker settles for its broader parent.

title: RCER: Reconstructing Cross-Evidence Relations for Iterative Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Iterative retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) accumulates knowledge from retrieved evidence to answer complex questions, but existing methods struggle to reconstruct entity correspondences and inferential dependencies across retrieved passages as new information emerges. We propose RCER, an iterative RAG method that reconstructs these cross-evidence relations directly from accumulated source passages. Inter-round relational evidence acquisition identifies entity correspondences and relational dependencies to drive dynamic problem decomposition and iterative retrieval. Reasoning context reconstruction independently constructs a coherent reasoning context through joint selection of complementary passages and derivation of cross-evidence inferences. Cross-evidence compositional reasoning leverages these inferences to establish entity correspondences and compose relations across selected passages for answer derivation. Experiments show that RCER outperforms the best baselines by 2.83 EM and 3.06 F1 points on average across three multi-hop QA benchmarks and achieves superior performance on narrative and implicit reasoning tasks.

title: Claw-Free and Line Graph Edge Deletion on Block Graphs
summary: Edge deletion problems ask for the fewest edges whose deletion gives a graph with a specified property. We study two such problems on block graphs. First making the graph claw-free, and second making it a line graph. Since every line graph is claw-free, the second problem is at least as difficult as the first. We show that on block graphs the two optimum values are always equal, and both are attained by the line graph of a forest. The main step is a completion argument, in which starting from any claw-free solution, we put back edges to get some nice structure inside each block still maintaining the claw-free property. This reduces both edge-deletion problems to the same problem of selecting vertices within the blocks of the input graph. We solve it by dynamic programming in $O(n+m)$ time, which also produces an optimal deletion set and a forest whose line graph is what remains after the completion argument. We also extend the method to $K_{1,r+1}$-free edge deletion for every fixed $r$.

title: Bounded-Density Vertex Deletion Beyond Vertex Cover
summary: We study \textsc{Bounded-Density Vertex Deletion} (BDVD), where one asks whether at most \(k\) vertices can be deleted so that every remaining subgraph has density at most a rational input threshold \(\tau_\rho\). We address the twin-cover and distance-to-cluster cases left open by Raupach, Breitkopf, Herrmann, and Nichterlein (MFCS 2026). We prove fixed-parameter tractability parameterized solely by the twin-cover number, for unrestricted input density. For distance to cluster, we establish fixed-parameter tractability parameterized by \(\operatorname{dc}(G)+\lfloor2\tau_\rho+1\rfloor\), and complement this with \(\mathsf{W[1]}\)-hardness parameterized by \(\operatorname{dc}(G)\) alone when the target density is part of the input, even for integral targets. Thus distance to cluster alone is fixed-parameter tractable throughout \(\tau_\rho<1\), while it is insufficient for unrestricted input density. Finally, we settle the combined parameter treewidth plus solution size, an open problem posed by Bazgan, Nichterlein, and Vazquez Alferez (JCSS 2025). We prove that BDVD is \(\mathsf{W[1]}\)-hard parameterized by \(\operatorname{td}(G)+k\), and hence also by \(\operatorname{tw}(G)+k\), already for targets strictly between \(1\) and \(2\).

title: Simple, Faster (min, +) Matrix Multiplication and APSP
summary: In this note, we provide a deterministic algorithm that computes the $(\min, +)$-Matrix Product $C = A * B$ of two $N \times N$ matrices $A$ and $B$ with polynomially bounded integer entries in $\tilde{O}(N^{2.9964})$ time, improving upon the exponent of $O(N^{2.9995})$ time obtained in the recent breakthrough by Anthropic (Alman and Vassilevska Williams, 2026). Our algorithm uses a phased approach first proposed by Bringmann, Grandoni, Saha, and Vassilevska Williams in 2016. The phased approach produces an approximation $\tilde{C}$ of $C$ in truly subcubic time such that the number of remaining triples $(i,k,j): A_{i,k}+B_{k,j} < \tilde{C}(i,j)$ is truly subcubic. This provided strong evidence that a truly subcubic $(\min, +)$-Matrix Product and therefore, a truly subcubic algorithm for All Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) may exist. However, to find the remaining triples in subcubic time, a sparse certificate is needed whose construction was not known. We use the thin matrix product theorem of the recent breakthrough to provide such a certificate. This gives a simple modular subcubic algorithm for APSP.

title: Subexponential Parameterized Approximation for Group-Fair Euclidean $k$-Center
summary: Clustering is a basic tool for grouping data into meaningful classes, but in many applications the resulting clusters must also respect the fairness conditions among different groups. We study this direction for the group-fair Euclidean $k$-center problem in fixed dimension, where the input points are partitioned into disjoint color classes, and every cluster must satisfy given lower and upper bounds on the fraction of each color. We give a separator-based recursive approximation algorithm for the continuous-center setting. The main idea is to first reduce the continuous search space to a finite candidate center set and then use the geometric sphere separators to break the instance into smaller subproblems. Our algorithm gives a bicriteria approximation: the clustering radius is within a factor of $(1+\epsilon)$ of the optimum exactly fair solution, while the fairness bounds are relaxed only by a multiplicative factor. For fixed dimension, number of colors, and approximation parameters, the running time is polynomial in input size and subexponential in $k$. A recent IJCAI-ECAI2026 result gives a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation for group-fair $k$-center in bounded doubling metrics with running time $(k/\epsilon)^{\mathcal{O}(k)}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$. In the fixed-dimensional Euclidean setting considered here, we improve the dependence on $k$ to subexponential, while allowing continuous centers. The fairness guarantees of the two results are different: the previous work allows an additive fairness violation, whereas our algorithm uses a controlled multiplicative relaxation.

title: An Analytic 0.48-Approximation for Non-Monotone k-Submodular Maximization under a Matroid Constraint
summary: We give a randomized polynomial-time $0.48$-approximation for maximizing a nonnegative non-monotone $k$-submodular function under a matroid constraint, for every $k\ge2$. The algorithm combines a top-two label rule with a nested-chain potential and maximum-weight matroid bases. Its analysis reduces the approximation guarantee to a one-dimensional time allocation: a uniform local lower bound leads to a linear differential equation, concavity closes the remaining interval, and two elementary budgets complete the proof. A strict saving in the time budget absorbs sampling and discretization errors, yielding the exact $0.48$ guarantee in the value-oracle model.

title: Undirected Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
summary: Network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages, whereas routing only forwards them. The Li-Li conjecture asserts that network coding and fractional routing have the same capacity region in undirected multiple-unicast networks. We give a counterexample to this conjecture and apply it to external-memory integer sorting. Since Aggarwal and Vitter posed the question in 1988, whether integer sorting can beat the external-memory comparison bound has remained a central and extensively studied open problem. We give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $\Theta(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is $O\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon}\right]\right)$, where $\varepsilon>0$ is an absolute constant. In a range of parameter regimes, this bound is asymptotically smaller than the classical comparison-sorting bound. We also use Lean 4 to verify the sorting algorithm's correctness and complexity bounds, and the strict advantage of coding over routing.

title: Towards Dynamic Top-$k$ Simple Shortest Paths
summary: Computing the top-$k$ \textit{simple} shortest paths between two vertices of a graph, i.e., solving the P-KSSP problem, is a fundamental primitive in graph analytics. In modern scenarios, however, queries are rarely one-shot: parameters change as applications adapt their information needs, and recomputing a solution from scratch at every request quickly becomes a bottleneck. We study P-KSSP in a dynamic setting, focusing on changes of the parameter $k$: given a top-$k$ solution for a pair of vertices and a new value $k'$, the goal is to compute a top-$k'$ solution reusing the previously computed paths. Our approach rests on the \textit{pseudo-tree}, a compact representation of a collection of simple $s$--$t$ paths: we show that building it from an arbitrary, unstructured solution amounts to trie construction, and give two constructions running in time linear in the size of the collection. On top of it, we design UPD, a dynamic algorithm that updates a solution upon a change of $k$; we prove its correctness, analyze its complexity, and show that it is a general, solver-agnostic scheme, which starts from the paths alone, is parametric in the routine that generates candidate paths and combinable with known preprocessing techniques, as well as with an online pruning rule that we formalize. While a worst-case update is asymptotically comparable to recomputing from scratch, an extensive experimental evaluation shows that a variant of UPD is the fastest method in the large majority of tested configurations, often by a wide margin (with speedups over recomputation that grow with $k$ and $k'$ and exceed $60\times$), yielding a practical recipe for the configuration to deploy.

title: Optimal Online Stochastic Matching
summary: We resolve the problem of unweighted online stochastic matching with a known arrival law by establishing its optimal competitive ratio. For Poisson arrivals, we achieve $1-e/e^e\approx0.8206$, matching the upper bound of Chierichetti, Giacchini, Panconesi, and Vattani [ICALP 2025]. For exactly $n$ i.i.d.~arrivals, we obtain the same guarantee up to an additive $O(n^{-1/2})$ loss. Our key technical contribution is an exact correspondence between Poisson matching and exponential scheduling, preserving both online performance and the expected offline optimum. To prove the latter, we show that the distribution of the maximum of a random supermodular set function is determined by its joint distributions along chains of nested sets, a result of independent interest. This reduces the analysis to chains, where classical Poisson--exponential duality applies. The offline equivalence extends to arbitrary nonnegative edge weights. We then design a posterior allocation policy for exponential scheduling and use the correspondence to transfer its optimal competitive guarantee to online matching. Additionally, we show that the optimal competitive ratio under an unknown arrival law is strictly lower than $1-e/e^e$, establishing a strict separation between the known and unknown arrival models.

title: Output-linear time enumeration of potential maximal cliques
comment: This paper was accepted at SODA 2027. 54 pages, 18 figures
summary: First defined by Bouchitté and Todinca, Potential Maximal Cliques (PMC) are a well studied notion in graph theory due to its numerous applications. The PMCs of an undirected graph $G$ are defined as the maximal cliques of the minimal triangulations of $G$. Their number can be exponential in the size of the graph. PMCs were crucial in the design of a polynomial-time algorithm which solves Maximum Weight Independent Set on $P_6$-free graphs (Grzesik, Klimošová, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk, 2020). They also play a central role in the proposal of a polynomial-time algorithm to solve Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth $\le t$ (Fomin, Todinca, Villanger, 2013). Last but not least, certainly one of the main application of PMCs is the existence of an exact dynamic-programming algorithm to determine the treewidth of a graph (Fomin, Kratsch, Todinca, Villanger, 2008) which uses its list of PMCs as an input. In fact, the enumeration of PMCs stands as the bottleneck for the computation of treewidth with this method: the PMC-enumeration step takes output-quadratic time (Bouchitté, Todinca, 2002) while the dynamic-programming one takes a time linear in the number of PMCs. This two-step procedure was proven to be among the most performing approaches in practice to determine treewidth. Answering a longstanding open question, we propose an algorithm to enumerate PMCs in output-linear time, {\em i.e.} a running time linear in the number of PMCs. This offers nice perspectives not only from the theoretical viewpoint - better running time for the PMC-based methods determining treewidth, for Minimum Fill-In and Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth $\le t$ - but also from the practical side, with the possibility to propose top-performance implementation.

title: Revisiting Non-Adaptive Set Membership Schemes: Removing the Logarithmic Factor
summary: We study non-adaptive bit-probe schemes for static set membership. Each query reads a fixed number of bits and answers by strict majority. We revisit the random bipartite-graph construction of Garg and Radhakrishnan [STACS, 2017]. The main observation is that a slightly stronger expansion property already bounds the number of exceptional elements. This makes a separate probabilistic estimate for exceptional elements unnecessary. A detailed union-bound calculation then gives, for every fixed $t\ge5$, a logarithm-free existence bound of $O_t(m^{1/c}n^{1-1/c})$, where $c=\lfloor(t-1)/2\rfloor$. For odd $t$, this removes the logarithmic factor from the general upper bound of Garg and Radhakrishnan [STACS, 2017].

title: Approximation Algorithms for Emergency Vertex Cover with Few Stations and Fault-Tolerant Coverage
summary: The Emergency Vertex Cover problem (Em-VC) assigns budgets to stations at graph vertices to cover every edge while minimizing the total budget. The cost of covering an edge from a station is the shortest-path distance from the station to the nearer endpoint plus the edge length. We study how restricting the number of stations affects the cost of ordinary and fault-tolerant coverage. In ordinary Em-VC, we prove that the optimal solution using at most two stations costs at most $5/4$ times the unrestricted optimum, improving the known $4/3$ guarantee for a single station. A recurrence extends this bound to larger station limits, giving approximation factors that converge to $\sqrt{5}-1$. Budget-threshold enumeration computes the restricted optimum in polynomial time for every fixed station limit. Under $k$-fold coverage, every edge must be covered by at least $k$ distinct stations, ensuring coverage after any $k-1$ station failures. We prove that selecting the $k$ vertices with the smallest full-coverage costs yields a $2$-approximation relative to the unrestricted optimum for $k$-fold coverage. When $k=2$, we combine upper bounds derived from the structure of the covering balls to improve the approximation guarantee to $5/3$.

title: Learning-Augmented Streaming Algorithms for Approximating Boolean Max-CSPs
summary: We study learning-augmented streaming algorithms for estimating the value of Boolean Maximum Constraint Satisfaction Problems (Max-CSPs). Specifically, we consider streaming algorithms equipped with an $\varepsilon$-accurate oracle: for each variable, the oracle outputs a label in $\{-1,1\}$ that agrees with a fixed optimal assignment with probability $1/2+\varepsilon$, and disagrees otherwise. Prior work by Dong, Peng, and Vakilian [ITCS 2025] showed that, for the special case of Max-Cut, such an oracle enables a $(1/2+\Omega(\varepsilon^2))$-approximation using $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ words of space in insertion-only streams, and $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,\log n)$ words of space in dynamic streams. We substantially generalize and strengthen their result, provided that a highly accurate estimate of $\varepsilon$ is available. For any Boolean Max-$2$CSP and any $\eta>0$ independent of $\varepsilon$, we obtain, with high constant probability, a single-pass $(1-\eta)$-approximation using $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,1/\eta)$ words of space in insertion-only streams, and $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,1/\eta,\log n)$ words of space in dynamic streams, where $n$ is the number of variables. We further extend our techniques to general Boolean Max-$k$CSPs for $k\ge 3$, with slightly worse space complexity.

title: With Leverage, the Gambler is Not the One Who Gets Ruined
summary: In this note we explore the following simple question: How does the classic \emph{gambler's ruin} phenomenon change if we allow the gambler \emph{financial leverage}? We show that, with a moderate amount of leverage, it is possible for an (idealized) gambler to sustain seemingly improbable profits over a remarkably long time horizon without ever going bankrupt, \emph{even} if the gambler makes only fair bets. With a leverage ratio of $L = 10$ (less than what Lehman Brothers Holdings had from 1995--2008), the probability of multiplying one's money by $1000\times$ without going bankrupt is roughly $50\%$. More generally, given $L$-fold leverage, and given the goal of multiplying one's money by a factor of $r > 1$, the optimal gambling strategy has probability roughly $r^{-1/L}$ of success. The results in this note are designed as part of the course development for the CMU randomized algorithms course.
